glycemic_index.title: Review your GI every day
glycemic_index.description:
GI (glycemic index) describes the blood glucose response to carbohydrates in a food compared with glucose. Lower GI generally means a smaller response to the same amount of available carbohydrate. Portion size, preparation, ripeness and the rest of the meal also matter. GI alone does not determine how healthy a food is.

Insulin sensitivity: Insulin helps cells take up glucose from the blood. With insulin resistance, cells respond less well to insulin. GI can help you choose carbohydrate sources with a lower glucose response as part of eating habits that support metabolic health. Some research reports improved insulin-resistance markers with lower-GI diets, but results vary. Low GI or reviewing a chart does not guarantee prevention of insulin resistance. Physical activity, sleep, overall diet and weight management when appropriate also matter.

Everyday choices: Vary fibre-rich carbohydrate sources such as pulses and whole grains, and consider portion sizes. Compare similar foods and preparations rather than simply chasing the lowest GI number.

Your daily goal has two parts in one nutrition tip: log at least one carbohydrate-containing meal with known GI, and open the GI page using the goal link once a day. Both parts are needed to complete today’s tip. Review the trend, period average and coverage. After five seconds with the page active, today’s review is recorded automatically. The goal is to review your eating habits, not to reach a specific GI. Add the tip to your plan to activate the goal.

Reading the data: Daily GI is weighted by carbohydrate amounts in entries with known GI. The period average is the mean of daily values with known GI. Coverage is the proportion of all logged carbohydrates with known GI. Low coverage means the average describes only part of what you logged. Missing GI is not zero, and carbohydrate-free foods do not need GI. Catalog references and AI estimates may contribute. Missing GI in older meals is not filled in automatically.

Sources: NIDDK, Insulin Resistance & Prediabetes; Yu et al. 2025 (PMID 40018272); Sacks et al. 2014, OmniCarb (PMID 25514303).

areas.energy: GI helps compare carbohydrate sources and understand estimated meal glucose responses. Review both the average and how much logged food has known GI.
areas.longevity: GI can support food choices for metabolic health. Insulin sensitivity depends on several habits; lower GI does not guarantee protection against insulin resistance.

profile_macro_goals.title: Follow your daily macro goals
profile_macro_goals.description:
Energy and nutrient needs depend on factors including age, body size, and physical activity. The app’s macro guide uses birth date, weight, height, biological sex, and physical activity level (PAL) to estimate energy needs. The selected distribution is then converted into grams of protein, carbohydrates, and fat, including the app’s age adjustment for protein.

Using this tip: Complete the automatic macro guide and save a preset distribution. This tip reads those exact saved goals and tracks the same amounts as the journal’s macro card. It does not add a separate protein target or additional amounts on top of your macros.

Custom goals: Manually entered macros, a custom energy intake, or a custom distribution do not activate this tip. A link to macro settings is shown instead. You can still use custom goals in ordinary macro tracking.

Food quality matters too: Protein, carbohydrates, and fat have different roles. Include varied protein sources, fiber-rich foods, and fat sources. Identical macro totals can come from meals with very different fiber, vitamin, and mineral content.

The calculation is an estimate, not an individualized medical prescription. Review the guide when weight or activity changes. Illness or special nutritional needs may require individual assessment. This tip is intended for adults aged 18 and over, including those aged 65+.

areas.longevity: A profile-calculated energy and macro plan can help structure food intake around age and activity. It complements food quality and regular habits; reaching gram totals is not itself a measure of long-term health.
areas.energy: Energy needs are estimated from body measurements, age, and PAL. Protein, carbohydrates, and fat all provide energy but have distinct roles. This tip follows saved guide targets without performing a separate calculation.
areas.strength: Protein contributes to muscle maintenance, while adequate energy supports training and recovery. The macro guide adjusts protein calculations for factors including age. Dietary targets do not replace resistance training.

targets.description: Daily protein, carbohydrate, and fat targets come from your completed automatic macro guide. Custom macros or a custom energy intake are not used for this tip. Edit and save the guide to update the targets.

protein_older_adults.title: Protein for adults aged 65+
protein_older_adults.description:
With increasing age, dietary protein often needs to provide a greater share of energy even when overall energy needs decrease. Swedish Food Agency guidance for older adults specifies 15–20% of energy from protein, approximately 1.2 grams per kilogram of body weight daily. Energy percentage refers to food energy, not the weight of the portion. This provides recommendation context, not a separate target in the app. Your target comes from saved macro settings, where the guide considers age, body measurements, and activity level (PAL).

Why it matters: Muscle responses to protein and exercise may become weaker with age, known as anabolic resistance. Digestion and the amount of meal-derived amino acids reaching muscles may also change, but absorption does not automatically decline in every older adult. Protein together with resistance training helps preserve muscle mass, strength, and daily function.

More protein in meals: Include a protein source at main meals and, where useful, snacks. Vary fish, eggs, dairy, poultry, beans, lentils, and soy foods. Breakfast could include eggs, quark, or yogurt. Legumes and whole grains together contribute protein and other nutrients.

With a small appetite: Smaller, more frequent meals may make adequate intake easier. Prioritize both energy and protein, adapting texture when chewing is difficult. Ordinary food is the starting point; protein powder or nutritional drinks are not required. Unintentional weight loss, swallowing difficulties, or persistently poor appetite warrant healthcare assessment.

Individual needs: Complete macro settings before tracking this target. An individually prescribed intake can be saved as manual macro goals. Kidney disease, other illness, malnutrition, or markedly different body weight may require a clinician or dietitian to adapt protein intake and the weight used for calculations. Follow individualized advice in those situations. Source for the protein reference: Swedish Food Agency, National Guidelines for Meals in Elderly Care.

areas.longevity: Adequate protein and energy help preserve muscle mass and function with age. This can support everyday independence and physical activity. The emphasis is food and muscle preservation, not evidence that protein itself extends lifespan.
areas.strength: With age, muscle protein synthesis may respond less strongly to a meal. Regular resistance training together with sufficient protein supports maintaining or building muscle. More protein does not replace the stimulus of exercise.

targets.description: This target is the same daily protein goal saved in your macro settings. Complete the macro guide using age, body measurements, and PAL, or save individually tailored manual macro goals. The tip does not create its own g/kg target or add extra protein on top of your macros.

ashwagandha_adaptogen.title: Ashwagandha
ashwagandha_adaptogen.description:
Evidence: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is a plant whose extracts contain compounds including withanolides. Small, short-term randomized trials of certain standardized extracts have reported reduced perceived stress and sometimes improved sleep compared with placebo. These findings cannot be generalized to every product or user.

Hypotheses: Effects on the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) stress axis have been proposed as one explanation. Some studies measured lower cortisol, but this does not prove that a “cortisol imbalance” was corrected or that the same mechanism applies to everyone. The role of withanolides remains under investigation.

User reports about emotional experience: Some people describe emotional blunting, with reduced positive and negative feelings, lower motivation or a reduced ability to experience pleasure (anhedonia). Some report that symptoms persist after stopping. These experiences deserve attention, but they do not establish how common this is, how long it may last or whether ashwagandha is the cause. Feeling emotionally blunted should not be equated with a desirable reduction in stress. Short follow-up in clinical trials means that possible persistent effects remain insufficiently studied.

Uncertainties: Larger, longer studies are needed. Benefits for immune function and sustained increases in energy are unproven.

Safety: Avoid during pregnancy, breastfeeding, before surgery and in people with autoimmune or thyroid disorders. Other chronic conditions, impaired kidney function or regular medication use require medical assessment; kidney transplant recipients also need approval from their transplant specialist. Long-term safety is unclear, and liver injury and drug interactions have been reported.

areas.nervousSystem: Some short-term studies report reduced perceived stress. Users also report emotional blunting, sometimes after stopping; its cause, frequency and duration remain uncertain.
areas.energy: Reduced fatigue has been reported in some studies, but a general, lasting energy-enhancing effect is unproven.
areas.immuneSupport: Immunomodulatory effects are investigated mainly in preclinical research. Clinically meaningful enhancement of immune function has not been established.

berberine.title: Berberine
berberine.description:
Origin: Berberine is an intensely yellow plant compound found in barberry species including Berberis aristata (Indian barberry) and Berberis vulgaris (common barberry), particularly in roots and bark. It contributes to the yellow colour of these plant parts. Berberine extracts should not be confused with the familiar ornamental hedge shrub Berberis thunbergii (Japanese barberry). Ornamental species can also contain berberine, but a garden shrub is not equivalent to a standardized extract.

Evidence: Berberine is a plant alkaloid studied mainly in people with type 2 diabetes and abnormal blood lipids. Some randomized trials report lower blood glucose, HbA1c and lipid levels, but study quality and results vary. Comparable benefits in healthy people have not been established.

Hypotheses: Cell and animal studies suggest that berberine affects mitochondrial energy production and activates the energy sensor AMPK. This may contribute to altered glucose metabolism, but does not establish that this mechanism explains clinical effects in humans.

Animal studies and autoimmunity: In mouse models of autoimmune arthritis and MS-like disease (experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, EAE), berberine reduced some disease signs and inflammatory markers. Changes in T cells have also been observed. These findings generate hypotheses about immune modulation, but do not establish that berberine is an effective or safe treatment for autoimmune diseases in humans.

Blood pressure: Berberine has also been investigated for high blood pressure. Some studies report reductions, but findings are inconsistent and the evidence is limited. A meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials in metabolic syndrome found no statistically significant effect on systolic or diastolic blood pressure. Berberine is therefore not an established treatment for hypertension and does not replace prescribed treatment.

Helicobacter pylori and stomach cancer: Persistent infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) can cause chronic stomach inflammation and increases the risk of stomach cancer. Most infected people do not develop cancer. Treatment that eradicates the infection can reduce the risk. Berberine has been studied as part of combination regimens with antibiotics and acid-suppressing medicines to eradicate H. pylori. Berberine alone has not been shown to prevent or treat stomach cancer and does not replace prescribed treatment for the infection.

Uncertainties: Trials are often short and use different preparations. Long-term effects on disease outcomes and lifespan are unproven.

Safety: Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding and do not give to infants. Kidney disease, organ transplantation or treatment with glucose-lowering medicines requires medical assessment. Berberine can affect blood glucose and increase tacrolimus and cyclosporine levels, with risks including kidney toxicity. People with autoimmune disease, particularly those receiving immunosuppressive treatment, should discuss use with their treating clinician. Before surgery, inform the surgical or anaesthesia team and follow their instructions about pausing use. Gastrointestinal symptoms and drug interactions can occur.

areas.digestiveHealth: Berberine has been studied in combination regimens for Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium that increases stomach cancer risk. Berberine alone has not been shown to eradicate the infection or prevent cancer.
areas.cardioFitness: Some studies report improved blood lipids in people with metabolic disorders. Effects on blood pressure remain uncertain, and a reduction in cardiovascular events has not been established.
areas.energy: Preclinical research suggests effects on AMPK and glucose metabolism. This is not evidence of increased perceived energy in healthy people.

brown_fat_cool_home.title: Brown fat and a cool home environment
brown_fat_cool_home.description: Brown fat helps the body burn energy and generate heat. Spending time in a cool indoor environment, ideally below 21°C (70°F), can stimulate brown fat activity and increase energy expenditure. Lowering the temperature at home occasionally may support metabolism and metabolic health.

areas.energy: Activation of brown fat increases energy expenditure and may support better metabolic health.

colorful_vegetables_anthocyanins.title: Eat a variety of colorful vegetables
colorful_vegetables_anthocyanins.description: Eating vegetables in a variety of colors, especially dark and red ones rich in anthocyanins, provides a broad spectrum of antioxidants and phytonutrients. Anthocyanins, found in foods like blueberries, red cabbage, and beets, have been shown to support heart health, reduce inflammation, and protect cells from oxidative stress. Vary your vegetable colors to maximize health benefits.

areas.nutrition: Colorful vegetables provide different vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants that strengthen the immune system and promote overall health.

eat_colorful_veggies.title: Eat colorful vegetables
eat_colorful_veggies.description: Eating vegetables in a variety of colors provides a broad spectrum of antioxidants and nutrients. Vary the colors on your plate to support digestion and immune function.

areas.digestiveHealth: Colorful vegetables support gut health and digestion.
areas.immuneSupport: Different colors provide different antioxidants that strengthen the immune system.

orange.details: Oranges provide vitamin C, hesperidin and fiber that support immunity, blood vessels and gut health.

strawberries.details: Strawberries provide vitamin C and polyphenols such as anthocyanins that help protect cells.

blackCurrants.details: Black currants are rich in anthocyanins and vitamin C, offering strong antioxidant support.

kale.details: Kale contains folate, vitamin K and minerals that support metabolic and immune function.

broccoli.details: Broccoli contributes fiber, vitamin C and sulfur compounds that support detox and gut health.

vitamin_d.title: Vitamin D
vitamin_d.description: Vitamin D levels can vary based on factors such as sun exposure, diet, and geographic location. Pairing D3 with complementary vitamin K2 helps route calcium to bones and protects soft tissues. Consider adding magnesium bisglycinate to support vitamin D activation and efficient calcium uptake.

areas.energy: Vitamin D supports mitochondrial function and cellular energy production by regulating calcium homeostasis.
areas.immuneSupport: Vitamin D modulates both innate and adaptive immune responses, with low levels associated with increased infection susceptibility.
areas.strength: Vitamin D is critical for muscle strength and function through calcium regulation and muscle protein synthesis pathways.
areas.nervousSystem: Vitamin D influences neurotransmitter production and has neuroprotective effects in the central nervous system.

sardines.details: Aim for a 120 g serving of salmon or mackerel 2-3 times per week (~400-600 IU vitamin D).

eggs.details: Two whole eggs supply roughly 80-100 IU vitamin D.

fortifiedDairy.details: A 250 ml glass of fortified milk or plant milk delivers about 100-130 IU vitamin D.

chanterelles.details: 100 g chanterelles provide around 400 IU vitamin D and are rich in potassium and iron.

vitamin_e_antioxidant_support.title: Vitamin E for antioxidant defense
vitamin_e_antioxidant_support.description: Vitamin E shields cell membranes from oxidative stress and supports cardiovascular resilience. Mixed tocopherols and tocotrienols cover a wider spectrum than alpha-tocopherol alone, making them useful when inflammatory or lipid stress is high. Combining with carotenoids like astaxanthin offers complementary membrane protection. Large doses of isolated alpha-tocopherol can crowd out other E forms, so stay near label guidance unless you are using mixed complexes.

areas.immuneSupport: Vitamin E enhances immune cell signaling and protects lipids in cell membranes from peroxidation.
areas.cardioFitness: Adequate vitamin E helps maintain endothelial function and balances oxidative load during exercise.
areas.energy: By preserving mitochondrial membranes, vitamin E supports efficient energy production under stress.

coq10.title: Mitokondrienäring
coq10.description: Vissa näringsämnen är involverade i mitokondriella processer relaterade till cellulär energiproduktion.

areas.energy: CoQ10 spelar en kritisk roll i den mitokondriella elektrontransportkedjan, vilket är avgörande för cellulär energiproduktion.
areas.immuneSupport: CoQ10 har antioxidantegenskaper som hjälper till att skydda celler från oxidativ stress och stödjer immunsystemets funktion.

cellular_energy_nad.title: NAD+
cellular_energy_nad.description: NAD+ (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide) is a critical coenzyme found in every cell of the body. It plays a key role in cellular energy metabolism, DNA repair, and maintaining overall cellular health. Precursors such as NMN, NR, or foundational niacin can sustain NAD+ levels when direct supplementation is not preferred.

areas.energy: NAD+ is essential for the mitochondrial processes that generate ATP, the primary energy currency of the cell.
areas.nervousSystem: NAD+ supports the nervous system by aiding in cellular repair and protecting neurons from oxidative stress.
areas.immuneSupport: NAD+ contributes to immune function by supporting cellular metabolism and repair mechanisms vital for immune cells.

sleep_timing_circadian.title: Sleep timing and circadian rhythm
sleep_timing_circadian.description: Synchronizing sleep with the body's natural circadian rhythm optimizes sleep quality and recovery. Consistent sleep and wake times help regulate hormone production and metabolism.

habitTargets.description: Tracked automatically from your logged sleep onset compared with the bedtime in your personal settings. The daily goal is met when the difference is at most 30 minutes.

areas.sleepQuality: Regular sleep rhythm improves sleep quality by strengthening the body's natural melatonin production.
areas.immuneSupport: Circadian synchronization supports immune function by optimizing the body's natural defense cycles.
areas.energy: Consistent sleep schedule regulates energy levels and reduces daytime fatigue.
areas.longevity: Stable circadian timing supports long-term metabolic, hormonal, and cognitive resilience, which are key factors for healthy aging.

calm_alertness_ltheanine.title: L-Theanine for calm focus
calm_alertness_ltheanine.description: L-Theanine is an amino acid naturally found in green tea. It promotes relaxation without drowsiness and enhances focus by increasing alpha brain waves and balancing neurotransmitters like GABA, dopamine, and serotonin.

areas.mind: L-Theanine improves concentration and attention while reducing stress and promoting a state of calm alertness.

neurotransmitter_ltyrosine.title: L-Tyrosine for mental performance
neurotransmitter_ltyrosine.description: L-Tyrosine is an amino acid that serves as a precursor to dopamine, norepinephrine, and adrenaline. It supports cognitive function, focus, and mental performance, especially during stressful situations.

areas.mind: L-Tyrosine improves concentration, attention, and cognitive performance by increasing the production of key neurotransmitters.

maintain_hydration.title: Maintain hydration
maintain_hydration.description: Consistent daily fluid intake supports circulation, temperature regulation, and immune defense function. Adequate hydration is fundamental for all bodily functions.

areas.immuneSupport: Hydration supports immune defense by promoting lymph circulation and nutrient transport to cells.
areas.energy: Adequate fluid maintains energy levels and reduces fatigue by optimizing cellular metabolism.
areas.cardioFitness: Hydration improves cardiovascular performance by maintaining blood volume and oxygen transport.

electrolytes_balance.title: Electrolytes – do you need supplements?
electrolytes_balance.description:
Most recreational exercisers do not need additional electrolytes. Water and normal food are usually sufficient. Electrolyte drinks and salt tablets are not an essential part of a regular workout, and sweating alone does not establish a deficiency. Extra salt may instead add to an already high intake and affect blood pressure.

Electrolytes such as sodium, potassium, magnesium and calcium are essential – but that does not mean more in supplement form is better.

Prolonged exercise in heat: Additional sodium and fluid may be relevant with substantial, sustained sweat losses – for example in ultrarunning, long cycling events or several hours of work in heat. Swedish Football Association guidance mentions electrolyte drinks as an option for sessions exceeding an hour in heat. This is not an automatic supplementation threshold: needs depend on sweat rate, temperature, intensity, duration and food and drink intake.

Sweat rate and testing: Before an ultra event, a sports dietitian can help develop an individual fluid and sodium plan. Weighing before and after a training session, accounting for fluid consumed and any urine, gives a rough estimate of fluid loss. A sweat test measuring sweat sodium concentration can additionally estimate salt loss. Test in conditions resembling the event; results vary with factors including heat acclimation and are not exact dosing instructions. Salt marks on clothing cannot determine how much sodium you need.

Blood pressure and Swedish dietary guidance: General Swedish advice is no more than 6 grams of salt per day for adults, approximately 2.4 grams of sodium, from all food and drink combined. This is an upper limit for the everyday diet, not a target to reach. High salt intake can raise blood pressure. Sea salt, “mineral-rich” salt and broth can also provide substantial sodium and are not automatically better for blood pressure than table salt. Major sweat losses during prolonged sport require separate assessment.

Avoid overdrinking: During long events, consuming more fluid than the body loses can dilute blood sodium and cause dangerous hyponatraemia. Electrolyte drinks or salt tablets do not make overdrinking safe. Worsening headache, nausea or confusion during or after an event should not be self-treated with more water or salt; confusion, seizures or reduced consciousness require emergency help.

Take particular care with hypertension, heart or kidney disease and medicines affecting fluids or electrolytes. Potassium supplements can be hazardous with impaired kidney function and certain medicines. Discuss supplementation with a healthcare professional.

areas.energy: With major sweat losses, individually adjusted fluid and sodium intake may support performance. Fatigue and cramps alone do not establish electrolyte deficiency.
areas.cardioFitness: Fluid loss can affect blood volume and circulation. Extra salt is not routinely needed and high sodium intake can raise blood pressure; prolonged sport in heat requires individual assessment.
areas.nervousSystem: Sodium, potassium, magnesium and calcium support normal nerve and muscle function. Both low and high levels can be harmful; supplementation is not automatically better.

coconutWater.details: Coconut water provides fluid and potassium, but composition varies and it is not automatically suitable for major sodium losses during endurance events.

potatoes.details: Potatoes are rich in potassium, one of the key minerals involved in muscle and nerve function.

dental_health_basics.title: Dental health basics
dental_health_basics.description: Basic oral care is one of the highest-return health habits. Regular brushing, cleaning between the teeth, reducing frequent sugar exposure, and supporting a healthier oral microbiome can lower caries risk, protect the gums, and preserve teeth long term. Frequent snacking is a major problem because the teeth are exposed to repeated acid attacks and less time to recover between meals, which raises caries risk even when the food itself does not seem extreme. Good chewing function and low oral inflammation also support digestion and overall health.

areas.immuneSupport: Healthier gums and lower oral inflammation reduce chronic immune burden and help maintain a more balanced inflammatory state. Bleeding gums can also make it easier for oral bacteria and inflammatory compounds to enter the bloodstream, and poor gum health has been associated with a higher long-term risk of cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease.
areas.digestiveHealth: Good dental health supports chewing, saliva production, and the first stage of digestion while reducing problems linked to an unhealthy oral microbiome.

habitTargets.description: Brush your teeth in the morning and at night.

vitamin_c_immunity.title: Vitamin C for immunity
vitamin_c_immunity.description: Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin found in fruits and vegetables. It is a powerful antioxidant that supports the immune system and protects cells from oxidative stress.

areas.immuneSupport: Vitamin C strengthens immune defense by supporting white blood cells and increasing the body's resistance to infections.

orange.details: One medium orange (~130 g) provides about 69 mg vitamin C and 3.1 g fiber (including 1.6 g fermentable fiber supporting Faecalibacterium).

bellPeppers.details: Half a cup raw red pepper (~75 g) gives about 95 mg vitamin C.

kiwi.details: One large kiwi (~75 g) provides about 70 mg vitamin C.

blackCurrants.details: Half a cup black currants (~85 g) provides roughly 40 mg vitamin C.

echinacea_herbs.title: Echinacea for immune support
echinacea_herbs.description: Echinacea is a flowering plant traditionally used to support immune function. It contains active compounds that may help the body's natural defense mechanisms and has been studied for its potential to reduce the duration and severity of common colds.

areas.immuneSupport: Echinacea stimulates immune cell activity and may help the body respond more effectively to infections and support overall immune resilience.

glynac.title: GlyNAC
glynac.description:
GlyNAC combines glycine and N-acetylcysteine (NAC). Glycine is an amino acid, and NAC can supply cysteine. Together with glutamate, these are building blocks for glutathione, which contributes to cellular protection against oxidative stress. The sulfur-group connection comes from cysteine’s sulfur; glycine does not contain sulfur.

Research: A small placebo-controlled trial in older adults reported improved glutathione status and some measures of oxidative stress, metabolism, and physical function after 16 weeks. Another trial in healthy older adults using two weeks of treatment found no general increase in total glutathione compared with placebo. Differences in participants, doses, and treatment duration limit comparisons.

Memory and brain: An open-label pilot trial in eight older adults reported improved cognitive test scores after 24 weeks of GlyNAC. It lacked a placebo group and cannot establish treatment effects. Larger controlled studies are needed to confirm the findings.

The hypothesis is that providing building blocks may support glutathione synthesis when their availability is limiting. This does not mean everyone is deficient or that more is always better. GlyNAC has not been established to rejuvenate people, extend human lifespan, or treat fatigue in healthy people. Glycine sleep studies do not themselves establish sleep benefits for the GlyNAC combination.

Safety: NAC may cause nausea and digestive discomfort and can amplify nitroglycerin-related blood-pressure reductions and headache. Discuss supplementation with a healthcare professional during medication use, chronic illness, pregnancy, or breastfeeding. The app does not set a general nutrition target for GlyNAC; research doses should not be interpreted as a personal recommendation.

areas.longevity: GlyNAC is being studied in healthy-aging research, focusing on glutathione, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and physical ability. Small human trials have reported improvements in some markers, while others found less clear effects. Changes in age-related markers do not establish slower biological aging or a longer life. GlyNAC is not an established treatment for extending human lifespan.
areas.mind: The small pilot trial assessed attention and executive function, including planning and switching between tasks. Improved test scores are promising but do not establish dementia prevention or general memory enhancement in healthy people.
areas.energy: Glycine and cysteine supplied by NAC are building blocks for glutathione. Glutathione participates in cellular redox regulation, which is closely linked to mitochondrial function. Small trials in older adults have examined whether GlyNAC affects glutathione status and energy metabolism, with varying findings. Increased everyday energy or ATP production in healthy people has not been established.
areas.immuneSupport: Glutathione participates in immune-cell function and responses to oxidative stress. GlyNAC is being studied as a way to supply glutathione precursors, but changes in laboratory markers do not themselves establish better immunity or fewer infections. Benefits may depend on baseline status and require further investigation.

muscle_leucine.title: Leucine for muscle synthesis
muscle_leucine.description: Leucine is the primary branched-chain amino acid that activates mTOR, the master regulator of muscle protein synthesis. Getting sufficient leucine, especially post-workout, is critical for building and maintaining muscle mass.

areas.strength: Leucine directly activates mTOR signaling, triggering muscle protein synthesis and recovery. A single dose of 3-5g post-workout stimulates muscle repair and growth by reducing protein breakdown.

chickenBreast.details: 120 g cooked chicken breast contains roughly 2-2.5 g leucine.

eggs.details: 3 large eggs provide about 1.8-2 g leucine.

bcaa_complex.title: Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs)
bcaa_complex.description: BCAAs—leucine, isoleucine, and valine—are essential amino acids that bypass liver metabolism and go directly to muscle. They support muscle protein synthesis, reduce fatigue, and aid recovery. The optimal ratio is roughly 2:1:1 (leucine:isoleucine:valine).

areas.strength: The BCAA ratio of 2:1:1 maximizes muscle protein synthesis and recovery. Leucine triggers mTOR, while isoleucine and valine reduce muscle breakdown — helping maintain mass during intense training blocks.
areas.cardioFitness: BCAAs reduce central fatigue, spare muscle glycogen during endurance sessions, and accelerate recovery between workouts by reducing delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS).

beef.details: 120 g lean beef contains a balanced BCAA profile (~5.5 g total BCAAs).

chicken.details: 120 g chicken breast has about 4.5-5 g total BCAAs.

eggs.details: 3 large eggs supply roughly 4.5-5 g BCAAs.

greekYogurt.details: 200 g Greek yogurt provides a strong BCAA profile, typically around 3.5-4.5 g total BCAAs.

arginine_pump.title: Arginine for blood flow and pump
arginine_pump.description: Arginine is a semi-essential amino acid that boosts nitric oxide (NO) production, increasing blood flow, nutrient delivery, and the muscle pump. It's especially effective taken pre-workout to enhance performance and vascularity.

areas.cardioFitness: Arginine increases nitric oxide production, which relaxes blood vessel walls, improving blood flow and cardiovascular efficiency.
areas.strength: Better blood flow enhances oxygen and nutrient delivery to muscles during training, supporting performance, strength, and the muscle pump.

pumpkinSeeds.details: 30 g pumpkin seeds provide about 2-2.5 g arginine.

sesameSeeds.details: 30 g sesame seeds contain roughly 1.5-2 g arginine.

almonds.details: 30 g almonds supply about 1-1.5 g arginine.

watermelon.details: A slice of watermelon (200 g) contains about 250-350 mg arginine, plus citrulline which converts to arginine.

leucine_rich_food.title: Leucine-rich whole foods
leucine_rich_food.description: Leucine is the key amino acid that triggers muscle protein synthesis via the mTOR pathway. Getting enough leucine from whole foods — chicken, fish, dairy, and eggs — is a practical way to support muscle building and recovery without relying solely on supplements.

areas.strength: A leucine threshold of roughly 2.5–3 g per meal activates mTOR and maximizes the anabolic response. Whole food sources like chicken breast, canned tuna, and Greek yogurt can reach this threshold in a normal serving.
areas.cardioFitness: Consistent leucine intake from whole foods preserves muscle mass during endurance training blocks and supports recovery between sessions.

canTuna.details: 150 g canned tuna delivers ~35 g protein with ~3 g leucine.

eggs.details: 3 large eggs supply ~18 g protein with ~1.5 g leucine.

greekYogurt.details: 200 g Greek yogurt provides ~20 g protein with ~1.8 g leucine.

cottageCheese.details: 200 g cottage cheese contains ~25 g protein with ~2 g leucine.

homocysteine_methylation_cardio.title: Methylation and cardiovascular support (homocysteine)
homocysteine_methylation_cardio.description:
Methylation transfers a methyl group between molecules. It is involved in gene regulation and the metabolism of many substances. Methionine is converted into S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), which donates methyl groups. This produces S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) and subsequently homocysteine. This is a regulated cycle – “more methylation” is not a general health goal.

Recycling with folate, B12 and TMG: Methionine synthase converts homocysteine back to methionine using vitamin B12 and methylfolate. MTHFR helps produce methylfolate and requires FAD derived from vitamin B2. An alternative pathway, mainly in the liver and kidneys, uses betaine (TMG) as a methyl donor through BHMT. Dietary choline can also be converted to betaine. These pathways interact but do not replace all of each other’s functions.

The glutathione connection: Homocysteine can also undergo transsulfuration to cysteine through B6-dependent enzymes. Cysteine can combine with glycine and glutamate to form glutathione. This explains the biological connection to glycine and NAC, but does not establish that everyone needs them alongside B vitamins. EGCG and selenium are not direct methyl donors, and the full supplement combination listed in this tip is not a clinically validated treatment.

Vascular health – associations and hypotheses: Elevated homocysteine is associated with vascular risk. Laboratory studies suggest oxidative stress, endothelial effects and reduced nitric oxide (NO) availability. An association or plausible mechanism does not establish that lowering it with supplements prevents disease. Homocysteine also reflects factors including B12/folate status and kidney function.

Human trials: In HOPE-2, 5,522 people with vascular disease or diabetes received B vitamins or placebo for approximately five years. Homocysteine fell, but the primary composite of cardiovascular death, heart attack and stroke did not improve; stroke was a favourable secondary outcome (Lonn and colleagues, 2006; PMID 16531613). In the Chinese CSPPT trial, first stroke fell from 3.4 to 2.7 percent with folic acid plus enalapril compared with enalapril alone over approximately 4.5 years (2015; PMID 25771069). This concerned hypertensive adults in a setting without mandatory folic acid fortification and cannot be directly generalised to everyone.

TMG and trade-offs: Betaine can lower homocysteine, but some randomised trials using gram doses also found increased LDL cholesterol (Olthof and colleagues, PLOS Medicine, 2005; DOI 10.1371/journal.pmed.0020135). Improving one laboratory marker does not automatically establish a net cardiovascular benefit. Such a supplement combination has also not been shown to extend human lifespan.

Practical use and safety: Start with a varied diet including folate-rich vegetables and legumes and appropriate sources of B12 and choline. Elevated homocysteine warrants assessment of the cause rather than simply adding several supplements. High folic acid doses can conceal blood changes from B12 deficiency while neurological damage continues. Chronically high B6 doses can cause peripheral neuropathy; EFSA’s adult upper limit is 12 mg per day, not a target dose. The tip’s nutrition targets do not prescribe supplements on top of dietary intake. Homocysteine lowering does not replace blood pressure or lipid treatment or smoking cessation.

areas.cardioFitness: Elevated homocysteine is associated with vascular risk and possible endothelial and NO-signalling disturbances. B vitamins can lower it, but large trials have not generally shown fewer heart attacks; some populations have experienced reduced stroke risk.
areas.longevity: One-carbon metabolism supports methylation and normal cellular function. Correcting nutrient deficiency matters, but extra methyl donors or lower homocysteine have not been shown to extend human lifespan.

salmon.details: Salmon supplies methionine, B vitamins, and omega-3s that support cardiovascular health when balanced with methylation cofactors.

collagen.title: Collagen for connective tissue
collagen.description: Collagen is a structural protein that supports joints, tendons, ligaments, skin, and bone matrix. Collagen peptides can be a practical way to support connective tissue resilience, especially together with a protein-rich diet and adequate vitamin C intake.

areas.strength: Collagen provides amino acids such as glycine and proline that support connective tissue structure in joints, tendons, ligaments, and bones.

chickenWings.details: A serving of chicken wings contributes collagen-rich connective tissue proteins.

citrulline_bloodflow_gut.title: Citrulline for blood flow and gut support
citrulline_bloodflow_gut.description: L-citrulline is an amino acid that can be converted into arginine and help raise nitric oxide production. It is best known for supporting circulation, endothelial function, and blood flow, which is why it is often used for cardiovascular performance and pump-related effects in training. For gut health, it is interesting because this same circulation support may help blood flow to the intestinal lining and help maintain barrier integrity during physiological stress, heavy training, or recovery. It is a more specialized supplement than fiber and probiotics, but can be relevant when the goal is to support both vascular function and mucosal resilience.

areas.digestiveHealth: By supporting arginine and nitric oxide availability, citrulline may help circulation and recovery processes in the intestinal mucosa.
areas.cardioFitness: Citrulline is most known for increasing nitric oxide availability, which can support endothelial function, blood flow, and cardiovascular performance.

watermelon.details: Watermelon is the best-known food source of citrulline, with the highest concentrations typically found in the white rind close to the peel.

cucumber.details: Cucumber contains small amounts of citrulline and can modestly contribute as part of a plant-rich diet.

glutathione.title: Glutathione for antioxidant defense
glutathione.description:
Glutathione is a small molecule built from the amino acids glutamate, cysteine, and glycine. It is present in many cells and participates in redox regulation, protection against peroxides, and metabolism of certain foreign compounds. Its function depends both on new synthesis and on recycling used glutathione.

Building blocks and synthesis: Two enzymatic steps join the amino acids and consume ATP. Magnesium is needed in these reactions. Cysteine can come from dietary protein or be formed through processes including B6-dependent conversion of homocysteine; NAC can supply cysteine. Glycine may also be limiting in some circumstances. A requirement for building blocks does not establish that supplementation always increases glutathione or improves health.

Selenium – using glutathione: Several glutathione peroxidases contain selenium within the amino acid selenocysteine. These enzymes use reduced glutathione (GSH) to detoxify hydrogen peroxide and other peroxides, producing oxidized glutathione (GSSG). Selenium is part of the enzyme, not the glutathione molecule. Deficiency can limit function, whereas additional selenium at adequate status does not automatically improve it.

B2 – recycling glutathione: Glutathione reductase converts GSSG back to GSH. It requires FAD, a coenzyme made from riboflavin (vitamin B2). Glutathione status therefore depends on functioning recycling as well as glycine and cysteine availability.

NADPH – electrons for recycling: Glutathione reductase uses NADPH as an electron donor to regenerate GSH. Cells produce NADPH through metabolic pathways including the pentose phosphate pathway. The NADP system is linked to niacin (B3), but NADPH is not the same as NADH or ATP. This is not a recommendation to take high-dose B3, NAD precursors, or consume more sugar to increase glutathione.

Zinc and surrounding defenses: Zinc is not a direct cofactor for glutathione reductase or selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidases. However, zinc and copper are present in superoxide dismutase (SOD1), which converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide. That peroxide can then be handled by glutathione peroxidase and catalase, among other systems. Antioxidant defenses form a network with distinct roles for different substances.

Practical implications: Adequate protein and a varied intake of vitamins and minerals support this system’s requirements. A biochemical relationship does not establish a need for a supplement combination of glutathione, NAC, selenium, zinc, and B vitamins. Excess selenium can be harmful, and prolonged high zinc intake can cause copper deficiency. Effects of glutathione supplements vary with formulation and context; changes in blood markers do not themselves establish better health.

areas.longevity: Glutathione is studied in aging research because redox balance, mitochondrial function, and responses to oxidative stress change with age. Small trials of glutathione precursors such as GlyNAC have examined some age-related markers, but these findings cannot be directly generalized to glutathione supplements. Glutathione supplementation has not been established to extend human lifespan or slow biological aging.
areas.immuneSupport: Immune cells use glutathione in redox regulation and peroxide handling. Several selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidases use GSH, while glutathione reductase recycles it using B2-derived FAD and NADPH. These are established biochemical functions, but do not establish that supplements strengthen immunity or prevent infections in adequately nourished people.
areas.energy: Glutathione contributes to redox balance, including within mitochondria. Synthesis consumes ATP, while recycling requires NADPH and B2-derived FAD. NADPH supplies electrons to antioxidant defenses and should not be equated with ATP powering energy-demanding work. The system is linked to cellular metabolism, but more supplemental glutathione does not automatically mean more energy.
areas.womenHealth: NAC, a glutathione precursor, has been studied in PCOS and endometriosis with possible but uncertain benefits. These findings do not establish the same benefits for glutathione supplements. NAC does not replace established treatment.

broccoli.details: Cruciferous vegetables provide sulfur compounds that support the body's own glutathione production.

avocado.details: Avocado provides antioxidant nutrients that can help maintain glutathione status.

spinach.details: Spinach contributes folate and plant antioxidants that support cellular redox balance.

box_breathing.title: Box breathing
box_breathing.description: Box breathing (also called square breathing) is a technique where you inhale, hold, exhale, and hold again for equal counts (typically 4-4-4-4). It's excellent for rapid stress relief and focus.

areas.nervousSystem: Box breathing creates a balanced rhythm that quickly activates the parasympathetic nervous system.
areas.immuneSupport: Regular practice helps reduce cortisol levels and supports immune resilience.

4_7_8_breathing.title: 4-7-8 breathing
4_7_8_breathing.description: The 4-7-8 technique involves inhaling for 4 counts, holding for 7 counts, and exhaling for 8 counts. It's particularly effective for relaxation and sleep preparation.

habitTargets.description: Mark when you have completed a comfortable 4-7-8 breathing exercise today.

areas.nervousSystem: The extended exhale activates the vagus nerve, promoting deep relaxation and reducing anxiety.
areas.sleepQuality: This technique is highly effective for preparing the body and mind for sleep, improving sleep quality.

alternate_nostril_breathing.title: Alternate nostril breathing
alternate_nostril_breathing.description: Nadi Shodhana (alternate nostril breathing) involves breathing through one nostril at a time in a controlled pattern. It balances the nervous system and enhances mental clarity.

habitTargets.description: Log today’s total minutes of alternate nostril breathing. The goal is three minutes per day.

areas.nervousSystem: This technique balances the left and right sides of the nervous system, promoting harmony and calm.
areas.mind: Alternate nostril breathing enhances mental clarity and concentration by balancing brain hemispheres.

diaphragmatic_breathing.title: Diaphragmatic breathing
diaphragmatic_breathing.description: Also called belly breathing or deep breathing, this technique focuses on breathing deeply into the abdomen rather than the chest. It's fundamental to all breathwork practices.

habitTargets.description: Log today’s total minutes of diaphragmatic breathing (belly breathing). The goal is five minutes per day.

areas.nervousSystem: Deep diaphragmatic breathing significantly reduces stress and anxiety by activating the relaxation response.
areas.energy: Proper oxygenation through diaphragmatic breathing improves energy levels and mental clarity.

sleep_duration_consistency.title: Sleep duration and consistency
sleep_duration_consistency.description: Getting 7-9 hours of consistent sleep each night is crucial for nervous system recovery, hormonal balance, and cellular repair. Maintaining a consistent sleep schedule helps regulate your circadian rhythm.

habitTargets.description: Aim for at least seven hours of sleep to support recovery.

areas.sleepQuality: Consistent 7-9 hours of sleep allows for complete sleep cycles, including deep sleep and REM sleep necessary for memory consolidation and emotional processing.
areas.energy: Adequate sleep duration directly impacts energy levels, cognitive function, and physical performance throughout the day.

sleep_environment_optimization.title: Sleep environment optimization
sleep_environment_optimization.description: Creating an optimal sleep environment is essential for quality sleep. This includes darkness, cool temperature, quiet conditions, and comfortable bedding that support restorative sleep.

habitTargets.description: Mark when you have prepared your sleep environment for the night, for example by darkening the room and reducing disruptive noise.

areas.sleepQuality: A dark, cool (60-67°F), quiet environment promotes melatonin production and deeper sleep cycles.
areas.nervousSystem: An optimized sleep environment reduces external stressors and allows the nervous system to fully relax and recover.

sleep_hygiene_practices.title: Sleep hygiene practices
sleep_hygiene_practices.description: Sleep hygiene encompasses daily habits that promote better sleep, such as avoiding caffeine in the afternoon, limiting screen time before bed, and maintaining regular exercise routines.

habitTargets.description: Mark when you have followed your chosen sleep hygiene habits today, for example avoiding late caffeine and limiting screen time before bed.

areas.sleepQuality: Good sleep hygiene practices remove barriers to quality sleep and create conditions for deeper, more restorative rest.
areas.immuneSupport: Quality sleep from good hygiene practices strengthens immune function and supports the body's ability to fight infections.

pre_sleep_wind_down.title: Pre-sleep wind-down routine
pre_sleep_wind_down.description: A structured wind-down routine 30-60 minutes before bed signals to your body that it's time to sleep. This can include relaxation techniques, light reading, meditation, or gentle stretching.

habitTargets.description: Answer Yes or No to all three questions about tonight’s wind-down. The goal is checked off once all questions are answered, including No answers.

areas.sleepQuality: A proper wind-down routine helps transition the nervous system from wakefulness to sleep, promoting faster sleep onset and deeper sleep.
areas.nervousSystem: Pre-sleep relaxation techniques activate the parasympathetic nervous system, preparing the body for restorative sleep.

sunlight_circadian.title: Morning sunlight exposure
sunlight_circadian.description:
Morning light gives the brain’s circadian clock a clear signal that the day has begun. With a typical daytime schedule, regular light after waking can help shift sleep timing earlier and support evening sleepiness. Effects depend on your biological timing, not just the time on the clock.

How it works: Light-sensitive retinal cells signal to the circadian clock in the hypothalamus. Light helps end the nighttime melatonin signal and increase alertness. Light reaching the eyes matters here, rather than UV exposure of the skin or vitamin D production.

Practical use: Go outside after waking when daylight is available, perhaps for a walk or breakfast outdoors. The app’s ten-minute target is a simple habit starting point, not a guaranteed biological dose. Intensity varies with season, cloud cover and surroundings. Even on cloudy days, outdoor light often provides a stronger daytime signal than dim indoor lighting.

Dark winter mornings: Use adequate lighting when you wake and take an opportunity to go outside when daylight arrives, for example during a break. Pair this with dim evening light to create a clear contrast between day and night.

You do not need to look towards the sun – look around normally. Keep eye protection and sunglasses when needed. Night work or significant circadian problems may require different timing; bright light therapy is a separate treatment.

habitTargets.description: Get at least ten minutes of natural morning light to support your circadian rhythm.

areas.sleepQuality: Morning sunlight exposure helps set your circadian clock, improving sleep quality and making it easier to fall asleep at night.
areas.nervousSystem: Natural light exposure regulates the nervous system by synchronizing circadian rhythms and supporting balanced cortisol production.
areas.energy: Morning sunlight boosts alertness and energy levels throughout the day by signaling to your body that it's time to be awake.
areas.immuneSupport: Regular circadian rhythm from sunlight exposure supports immune function and overall health.

cold_exposure_ans.title: Cold exposure therapy
cold_exposure_ans.description: Deliberate cold exposure, such as cold showers, ice baths, or cold plunges, activates the sympathetic nervous system and builds stress resilience. Regular cold exposure improves immune function, increases energy, and enhances mental clarity.

areas.nervousSystem: Cold exposure trains the nervous system to handle stress by activating and then balancing the sympathetic and parasympathetic responses.
areas.immuneSupport: Regular cold exposure has been shown to increase white blood cell count and strengthen immune function.
areas.energy: Cold exposure boosts dopamine and norepinephrine levels, leading to increased alertness, energy, and mood elevation.

meditation_mindfulness.title: Meditation and mindfulness
meditation_mindfulness.description: Regular meditation and mindfulness practices train the mind to stay present and reduce stress. These practices activate the parasympathetic nervous system, improve emotional regulation, and enhance cognitive function.

habitTargets.description: Meditate or practice mindfulness for at least ten minutes.

areas.nervousSystem: Meditation activates the parasympathetic nervous system, reducing stress hormones like cortisol and promoting deep relaxation and nervous system recovery.
areas.immuneSupport: Regular meditation has been shown to reduce inflammation, strengthen immune response, and improve overall health markers.
areas.mind: Mindfulness practices improve attention span, working memory, and cognitive flexibility by strengthening neural pathways associated with focus and awareness.
areas.longevity: Lower chronic stress and better autonomic balance are associated with reduced allostatic load and improved long-term healthspan.

nature_parasympathetic.title: Forest bathing
nature_parasympathetic.description:
Time in nature can create space for recovery, movement and a break from everyday demands. Forest bathing, or shinrin-yoku in Japanese, means taking in the forest atmosphere through the senses. The term was introduced in Japan in 1982. It centres on calm attention rather than bathing in water or achieving a hiking goal.

How to try it: Choose somewhere you feel safe. Walk slowly or sit for a while, noticing light between the trees, birdsong, scents and the texture of the ground. Put your phone aside and breathe normally without forcing it. Start with a short visit; a park or nearby green space can also make everyday nature contact accessible.

Research findings: Park and colleagues studied 280 young adults in field experiments across 24 Japanese forests. Short periods of walking and sitting in forests, compared with urban settings, produced lower cortisol, pulse and blood pressure and HRV patterns consistent with greater parasympathetic activity (2010; PMID 19568835). These are primarily short-term findings. Small samples, expectations, noise, movement and differences between settings make it difficult to isolate causes and establish how long effects last.

Immunity and forest scents: Small studies, including one involving twelve men, reported increased NK-cell activity after multi-day forest visits (Li and colleagues, 2007; PMID 17903349). Volatile plant compounds, sometimes called phytoncides, and reduced stress have been proposed as mechanisms. This does not establish fewer infections or lower cancer risk in humans.

The weekly target: White and colleagues found an association between at least 120 minutes of nature contact per week and better self-reported health and well-being (2019; PMID 31197192). This observational study does not establish a medical minimum. The app’s two hours are a practical habit target that can be spread across several visits. Adapt to your capacity, access and weather – recovery should not become another performance demand.

habitTargets.description: Spend at least two hours in nature during the week.

areas.nervousSystem: Quiet nature contact may reduce perceived stress. Some field studies show lower pulse and HRV changes consistent with parasympathetic recovery, but responses vary and do not establish guaranteed vagus nerve “activation”.
areas.immuneSupport: Small studies report changes in NK-cell activity after forest visits. These are preliminary biomarker findings, not evidence that forest bathing prevents infections or cancer.
areas.energy: Nature contact can offer a break from demanding stimuli and support gentle movement and mental recovery. Changes in perceived energy or calmness vary.

hrv_recovery_monitoring.title: HRV and recovery monitoring
hrv_recovery_monitoring.description: Heart Rate Variability (HRV) is a key metric for tracking nervous system balance and recovery status. Monitoring HRV helps optimize training intensity, prevent overtraining, and ensure adequate recovery between workouts.

areas.nervousSystem: HRV reflects the balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system activity, indicating stress and recovery levels.

areas.energy: HRV tracking helps identify when the body needs rest, preventing fatigue and optimizing energy management.
areas.cardioFitness: Monitoring HRV helps optimize cardiovascular training by ensuring adequate recovery between high-intensity sessions.
areas.strength: HRV data guides training decisions, helping prevent overtraining and optimize muscle recovery and performance gains.
areas.longevity: Tracking recovery helps maintain sustainable training and lower chronic stress burden, both important for long-term health and functional aging.

social_connection_vagal.title: Social connection and belonging
social_connection_vagal.description:
Social connection involves both having people around and feeling belonging, safety and reciprocal support. Social isolation describes limited contact, whereas loneliness is the feeling that relationships do not meet one’s needs. Someone can feel lonely in a large network or enjoy substantial time alone. Relationship quality therefore matters, not just the number of encounters.

Research findings: Holt-Lunstad and colleagues combined 148 studies with over 308,000 participants and found stronger relationships associated with better survival during follow-up (PLOS Medicine, 2010; PMID 20668659). Wang and colleagues analysed 90 prospective cohort studies involving approximately 2.2 million participants: isolation was associated with around 32 percent higher relative mortality and loneliness with approximately 14 percent (Nature Human Behaviour, 2023; PMID 37337095). These are population associations, not individual predictions or proof that a particular number of conversations extends life. Illness can also make maintaining relationships harder.

Possible mechanisms: Supportive relationships may provide practical help, support activity and sleep, and buffer perceived stress. In a small experiment involving 37 healthy men, support from a friend reduced the cortisol response to a standardised stress test (Heinrichs and colleagues, 2003; PMID 14675803). A meta-analysis of 41 studies also found a small association between social support and lower inflammatory markers (Uchino and colleagues, 2018; PMID 29565600). This does not mean contact always lowers cortisol, measurably activates the vagus nerve or “boosts immunity”.

Blue Zones: The term refers to regions where unusually high longevity has been reported, such as parts of Sardinia. Community and participation in family and local life are often proposed as contributing factors. In a study of 160 older adults in the Sardinian Blue Zone, satisfaction with social ties was associated with better self-reported psychological well-being (2018; PMID 29495425). This does not demonstrate that relationships caused the region’s longevity. Diet, activity, socioeconomic circumstances, genetics and the quality of population records also need consideration; Blue Zones are not a proven longevity formula.

Practical use: The habit target primarily means meeting in real life (IRL), for example during a walk, shared meal or community activity. Prioritise personal, reciprocal contact where you listen and take part in each other’s lives. Reading forums, scrolling or posting occasional comments does not count as this kind of meeting. A personal phone or video call can be an alternative when distance, health or other circumstances make meeting difficult; online relationships can also be meaningful. Consistency and reciprocity may be more useful than collecting many superficial contacts. The app’s two contacts per week are a simple habit starting point, not a scientifically established minimum. Adapt to your capacity and needs; relationships marked by conflict or insecurity can instead be stressful.

habitTargets.description: Have two meaningful social contacts during the week, preferably by meeting in person.

areas.nervousSystem: Supportive relationships can buffer perceived stress and influence physiological stress responses. The vagus nerve participates in autonomic regulation, but social contact is not a direct measure or guaranteed training of “vagal tone”.
areas.immuneSupport: Studies show a small association between social support and lower inflammatory markers. This is a possible link between relationships and health, not proof that more contact prevents infections or generally boosts immunity.
areas.energy: Meaningful relationships may provide emotional support and facilitate recovery, sleep and activity. Effects on perceived energy vary; safety and relationship quality matter.

calming_music_waves.title: Calming music and sound therapy
calming_music_waves.description: Listening to calming music, binaural beats, or nature sounds can reduce stress, lower heart rate, and activate the parasympathetic nervous system. Sound therapy has been used for centuries to promote relaxation and healing.

areas.nervousSystem: Calming music and sound therapy activate the parasympathetic nervous system, reducing stress hormones and promoting deep relaxation.
areas.sleepQuality: Listening to calming sounds before bed can improve sleep onset, increase deep sleep duration, and enhance overall sleep quality.
areas.mind: Certain frequencies like binaural beats and nature sounds can enhance concentration, reduce mental fatigue, and improve cognitive performance.

neuromuscular_training.title: Neuromuscular training concepts
neuromuscular_training.description: Neuromuscular training focuses on improving the connection between the nervous system and muscles to enhance strength, coordination, and overall performance.

areas.strength: Neuromuscular training enhances muscle strength and coordination, improving physical performance.
areas.cardioFitness: This training supports cardiovascular fitness by improving endurance and oxygen utilization during physical activity.
areas.nervousSystem: Neuromuscular training strengthens the communication between the nervous system and muscles, optimizing movement efficiency.

creatine_atp_strength.title: Creatine
creatine_atp_strength.description: Creatine is a naturally occurring compound that supports ATP production, the primary energy source for muscle contractions and brain function. It enhances strength, power output, mental clarity, and muscle recovery during intense training.

areas.strength: Creatine increases phosphocreatine stores in muscles, enhancing ATP production and improving strength and power output during high-intensity exercise.
areas.energy: Creatine supports cellular energy production by replenishing ATP more rapidly, sustaining energy during intense physical activity.
areas.cardioFitness: Creatine may support cardiovascular endurance by improving oxygen utilization and reducing fatigue during sustained aerobic activities.
areas.mind: Creatine supports brain energy metabolism and cognitive function, improving mental clarity, focus, and memory.

shilajit_performance.title: Shilajit for performance
shilajit_performance.description: Shilajit is a mineral-rich substance found in the Himalayas that supports mitochondrial function, enhances energy production, and improves physical performance. It contains fulvic acid and over 85 minerals in ionic form.

areas.strength: Shilajit supports muscle recovery, reduces exercise-induced muscle damage, and enhances strength and endurance.
areas.energy: Shilajit boosts mitochondrial ATP production, increasing cellular energy and reducing fatigue during physical activity.
areas.cardioFitness: Shilajit improves oxygen utilization and cardiovascular efficiency, enhancing aerobic capacity and endurance performance.

lactobacillus_reuteri.title: Lactobacillus reuteri
lactobacillus_reuteri.description: Lactobacillus reuteri is a probiotic bacterial strain studied for gut balance, immune signaling, support of the intestinal barrier, and parts of oral health. Effects are strain-specific, but certain L. reuteri strains may help reduce digestive discomfort, support a more resilient gut ecosystem, and potentially contribute to a healthier oral microbiome linked to lower caries risk and better gum balance.

areas.digestiveHealth: L. reuteri may support gut barrier function, reduce microbial imbalance, and help with bloating or digestive discomfort in some people.
areas.immuneSupport: By interacting with the gut immune system, L. reuteri may help support more balanced immune signaling and lower excessive inflammatory tone. Some strains are also studied for oral immune balance and reduced growth of bacteria associated with caries and gum irritation.

resistant_starch_barrier.title: Resistant starch, the gut barrier and butyrate
resistant_starch_barrier.description:
Resistant starch escapes digestion in the small intestine and can feed bacteria in the colon. It occurs in less ripe, green bananas. Cooling cooked pasta or potatoes can reorganise some starch into a less digestible form called retrograded starch. Some can remain after reheating. Freshly cooked pasta may also contain resistant starch; cooling does not guarantee a fixed increase. Amounts vary; cold pasta is still carbohydrate-rich food.

Butyrate and the gut barrier: Bacteria can ferment resistant starch into short-chain fatty acids including butyrate. Mature colon cells use butyrate as fuel, and experiments show effects on barrier function and immune signalling. Bacteria cooperate in breakdown and responses vary between people (2016; PMID 27357127). This is not a treatment for inflammatory bowel disease.

Weekly target: Eat green banana, cooked cooled potatoes, cold pasta or cold rice at three meals per week. AI analysis counts meals containing these sources in nutrition tracking. Food that was cooled and then reheated also counts. Specify in the description or ingredient list that potatoes, pasta or rice are cold/cooled or reheated after cooling, since this history cannot reliably be established from the image. Each meal counts once even if it contains several qualifying foods. Three times weekly is a simple habit starting point, not an established dose for the gut barrier.

Start with small amounts according to tolerance. Cool cooked food promptly and refrigerate at around 4 °C; do not leave pasta or potatoes out for hours to produce resistant starch. The Swedish Food Agency warns that organisms including Bacillus cereus can produce heat-stable toxins when food is stored incorrectly.

areas.digestiveHealth: Resistant starch can provide bacterial substrates for butyrate formation. Butyrate fuels mature colon cells and participates in gut barrier function.
areas.immuneSupport: Butyrate affects immune signalling in experiments. This provides a possible link to intestinal immune regulation, but the habit target is not a proven treatment for inflammation.
