Note: during AI analysis, check that preparation is identified as cold/cooled or reheated after cooling, and correct it if needed. Freshly cooked or heated food without earlier cooling does not count.

fiber_total_intake.title: Increase your fibre intake
fiber_total_intake.description:
The next step is to increase total fibre from varied foods. Swedish advice commonly recommends 25–35 grams daily for adults; the app target is 30 grams. This is total intake from daily food, not a requirement for fibre powder.

Choose whole grains, oats, legumes, fruit and vegetables. Fibres differ: some add bulk, others form gels or are fermented by gut bacteria. Fibre does not all need to be resistant starch.

Increase gradually and spread intake across meals. Adapt to digestive tolerance and drink enough. With IBS or other bowel symptoms, a dietitian can help tailor amounts and types.

areas.digestiveHealth: A varied fibre intake supports normal bowel function. Increase gradually and adapt to tolerance.

oats.details: Oats provide fermentable beta-glucans. Amounts vary between products.

soybeans.details: Soybeans provide several fibre types, including fermentable oligosaccharides.

fiber_butyrate.title: Fermentable fibres, acetate and propionate
fiber_butyrate.description:
Fermentable fibres feed intestinal microorganisms, producing acetate, propionate, butyrate and gases. This tip focuses on fibre sources beyond the resistant starch covered in the introductory tip. Total fibre is tracked in the separate level 2 tip.

Acetate and propionate: Many bacteria produce acetate, which can be used in metabolism or by other bacteria to produce butyrate. Propionate is largely handled by the liver. Both participate in receptor signalling, including FFAR2 and FFAR3, investigated for links to gut function, satiety and metabolism. This does not establish that a particular fibre reliably reduces appetite, blood glucose or weight.

Different fibres: Inulin and fructooligosaccharides occur in onions and chicory, galactooligosaccharides in legumes, beta-glucans in oats and barley, and pectin in fruit. Bacteria cooperate through cross-feeding, using each other’s breakdown products. Solubility, gel formation and fermentability are distinct properties.

Human studies show different responses to different fibres: a study involving 174 people found different microbiome and fatty acid responses to resistant starches and inulin (2019; PMID 30696735). Another found different starch structures could direct production towards propionate or butyrate (2020; PMID 32004499). Faecal fatty acids reflect what remains after absorption, not total production.

Practical use: Vary legumes, whole grains, oats, fruit and vegetables. This target concerns fermentable fibre only: 15 grams daily as an app planning target, not an official Swedish recommendation or a defined acetate amount. Increase gradually according to tolerance; inulin and other rapidly fermented fibres may cause gas and pain, particularly with IBS.

areas.digestiveHealth: Fermentable fibres produce different mixtures of acetate, propionate and butyrate. Microbial cooperation and fibre structure influence the result.
areas.immuneSupport: Short-chain fatty acids participate in signalling between microbes, gut cells and the immune system. Clinical effects of specific fibres require separate assessment.
areas.longevity: Acetate and propionate are studied for links to metabolism and ageing. Increasing one fatty acid has not been shown to extend human lifespan.

oats.details: Oats provide fermentable beta-glucans. Amounts vary between products.

soybeans.details: Soybeans provide several fibre types, including fermentable oligosaccharides.

chicoryRoot.details: Chicory root provides inulin. Concentrated products may cause gas; start cautiously.

oat_barley_beta_glucans_ldl.title: Beta-glucans for lower LDL
oat_barley_beta_glucans_ldl.description:
Beta-glucans from oats and barley are soluble, viscous fibers that can help lower LDL cholesterol. They form a gel in the gut and can reduce bile acid reabsorption, increasing the liver’s use of cholesterol to make new bile acids. Effects depend on dose, viscosity and food processing.

The daily target is 3 g of oat or barley beta-glucans, the amount underlying European cholesterol health claims. This means beta-glucans, not the weight of oats or total fiber. The LDL evidence concerns oats and barley. Mushroom and yeast beta-glucans have a different structure and cannot be assumed to have the same effect (EFSA, 2010; doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2010.1885).

Choose foods such as oats, oat bran or barley products. The amount needed depends on the product’s beta-glucan content; prefer declared values when available. The catalog’s oat value is an estimate, and dry oats must not be confused with the same weight of cooked porridge. Intake can be spread across meals. Increase gradually according to tolerance.

This target supports regular intake, not a guaranteed LDL reduction. Effects should be assessed with blood tests and also depend on the rest of the diet.
oat_barley_beta_glucans_ldl.targetDescription: Consume 3 g of oat or barley beta-glucans daily. Count beta-glucans themselves, not total fiber or food weight.

areas.longevity: Oat and barley beta-glucans can lower LDL, an established cardiovascular risk factor. This does not promise a particular lifespan.
areas.digestiveHealth: Beta-glucans bind water and can be fermented by gut bacteria. Increase gradually if prone to gas.

oatBran.details: Oat bran can be used in porridge, yogurt or baking. The reference value is 6.5 g beta-glucans per 100 g dry oat bran; about 47 g then provides just over 3 g beta-glucans. Other products can differ – check the package. Weigh the bran before cooking.

oats.details: Oats contain beta-glucans. The catalog uses an estimated 4.4 g per 100 g dry oats; the amount varies by product and variety. Prefer declared package values when available.

psyllium_ldl.title: Psyllium for lower LDL
psyllium_ldl.description:
Psyllium husk contains water-binding, gel-forming fibers, predominantly arabinoxylans rather than beta-glucans. The gel can reduce bile acid reabsorption and help lower LDL cholesterol.

A meta-analysis of 28 randomised trials found an average LDL reduction of about 0.33 mmol/L at a median dose of 10.2 g psyllium daily. Results varied between studies and individuals. The app instead tracks 5.2 g gel-forming psyllium fiber daily. This corresponds to about 10 g dry husk using the catalog estimate of 52 percent gel-forming fiber. This is a tracking conversion, not a separately established scientific fiber dose (2018; PMID 30239559).

Start with a smaller amount and increase gradually according to tolerance. Intake can be divided throughout the day. Mix with enough liquid and drink promptly according to product instructions; never swallow the husk dry. For mixtures, count only the psyllium husk fraction rather than the entire product weight.

Psyllium can affect medicine absorption; follow the package’s spacing instructions and ask a pharmacist if taking medicines. Do not use with swallowing difficulties or suspected intestinal narrowing or obstruction without medical assessment. Assess LDL effects through blood tests; this does not replace prescribed treatment.
psyllium_ldl.targetDescription: Aim for 5.2 g gel-forming psyllium fiber daily, corresponding to about 10 g dry husk using the app estimate. If your package specifies 1 tsp = 2.5 g husk, this provides about 1.3 g gel-forming psyllium fiber using that estimate. Teaspoon weights vary – check the package or weigh the amount and enter grams when logging. Start lower, increase gradually and follow the product instructions for fluid and dosing.

areas.longevity: Psyllium can moderately reduce LDL, which is relevant to cardiovascular health but does not establish longer lifespan.
areas.digestiveHealth: Psyllium retains water and can improve stool consistency. Adequate fluid and gradual increases are important.

psylliumHusk.details: Enter dry psyllium husk weight. The catalog estimates 52 percent as gel-forming psyllium fiber: 2.5 g husk provides 1.3 g, 5 g provides 2.6 g and 10 g provides 5.2 g. The target uses the same fiber value as the nutrition analysis. Water added for soaking does not count. Weigh the amount; teaspoon weights vary between products.

fiber_non_gel_forming_focus.title: Non-gel-forming fiber focus
fiber_non_gel_forming_focus.description: Non-gel-forming fibers are bulk-forming structural fibers that increase stool mass and speed colonic transit. This is important because shorter transit time reduces how long the gut lining is exposed to potentially harmful breakdown products and supports regular bowel emptying. Aim for 30 g total fiber and around 20 g non-gel-forming fiber daily.

areas.digestiveHealth: Cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and arabinoxylan support bowel regularity by adding stool bulk and reducing transit time, lowering constipation risk and bloating.
areas.immuneSupport: Regular bowel transit may reduce local inflammatory pressure by limiting mucosal contact with irritating residues, supporting a healthier gut environment for immune balance.
areas.longevity: Consistent intake of structural fibers supports long-term bowel function, healthier transit patterns, and lower risk patterns linked to colorectal disease.

almonds.details: Almonds are rich in insoluble fibers that support regular bowel movements and overall digestive health.

broccoli.details: Broccoli contains insoluble fibers that support regular bowel movements and overall digestive health.

kale.details: Leafy greens provide insoluble structural fibers that support bowel movement regularity.

plant_diversity_30_week.title: 30 different plants per week
plant_diversity_30_week.description: Aim for at least 30 different plant foods per week (vegetables, berries, fruits, legumes, nuts, seeds, herbs, and whole grains). Higher plant diversity is linked to a more diverse and resilient microbiome. How to fulfill it: count each unique plant once per week, and use mixed meals to increase variety fast.

areas.digestiveHealth: A wider range of plant fibers and polyphenols feeds more microbial species, which can improve stool quality, gut barrier support, and digestive resilience.
areas.immuneSupport: Greater microbiome diversity is associated with better immune signaling balance and lower chronic inflammatory tone.
areas.longevity: Weekly plant diversity is linked to better metabolic and inflammatory profiles, both relevant for healthy aging.

legumes.details: Use 2-3 different legumes weekly (for example lentils, chickpeas, black beans). Each counts as one unique plant.

kale.details: Swap between spinach, kale, arugula, romaine, and herbs instead of repeating one green every day.

fish_omega3_weekly.title: Fish meals for omega-3 and heart health
fish_omega3_weekly.description: Aim for 3 fish meals per week, with at least 1 fatty fish meal rich in EPA and DHA omega-3 fats. Omega-3 fatty acids support cardiovascular health, reduce inflammation, and promote brain function. Fatty fish like salmon, mackerel, and sardines are the most bioavailable sources.

areas.cardioFitness: Omega-3 fats reduce triglycerides, support healthy blood pressure, and improve endothelial function for cardiovascular resilience.
areas.mind: EPA and DHA are structural components of brain cell membranes and support cognitive function, mood regulation, and neuroprotection.
areas.immuneSupport: Omega-3 fats actively reduce systemic inflammation by modulating immune signaling and shifting the inflammatory balance toward resolution.

sardines.details: 100 g sardines provides about ~1.5 g EPA+DHA; excellent omega-3 source with easy canned options.

canTuna.details: Convenient option with similar omega-3 content to fresh fish. Often packed in oil for added omega-3s.

preparation.details: Baking, steaming, or poaching preserve omega-3s. Frying at high heat can damage delicate fats; use moderate heat or eat raw (sushi).

quantity.details: 120–150 g fish meal (roughly a palm-sized fillet) provides meaningful omega-3 intake. Higher frequency compensates for smaller portions.

polyphenol_microbiome.title: Polyphenols and microbiome health
polyphenol_microbiome.description: Polyphenols are plant compounds that act as prebiotics, selectively feeding beneficial gut bacteria. A high polyphenol intake supports microbiome diversity, reduces gut inflammation, and protects against oxidative stress.

areas.digestiveHealth: Polyphenols are partially metabolized by gut bacteria, producing bioactive metabolites that protect the gut lining and support microbiome balance.
areas.immuneSupport: Polyphenol metabolites regulate immune signaling and reduce systemic inflammation through interactions with the gut-immune axis.
areas.longevity: Higher polyphenol intake is associated with lower oxidative damage, reduced inflammation, and improved markers of healthy aging.

darkChocolate.details: 30 g dark chocolate supplies approximately 200–400 mg polyphenols, mainly flavanols and catechins.

blackCurrants.details: Half a cup black currants (~85 g) supplies roughly 300-400 mg polyphenols including anthocyanins and flavonoids.

pomegranate.details: Half a pomegranate (~150 g) contains around 400 mg polyphenols including ellagitannins.

extraVirginOliveOil.details: 2 tablespoons EVOO (~30 ml) supply roughly 30–50 mg polyphenols including oleocanthal.

milk_thistle_liver.title: Milk thistle for liver health
milk_thistle_liver.description: Milk thistle contains silymarin, a powerful antioxidant that protects liver cells, supports detoxification, and promotes liver regeneration. It's particularly beneficial for liver health and digestive function.

areas.digestiveHealth: Milk thistle supports bile production and liver function, improving fat digestion and overall digestive health.
areas.immuneSupport: By supporting liver detoxification, milk thistle reduces toxic burden on the body and strengthens overall immune resilience.

hiit_vo2max.title: HIIT for VO2 max
hiit_vo2max.description: High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) is one of the most effective methods to improve VO2 max, the maximum amount of oxygen your body can use during exercise. Unlike Zone 2, which mainly builds more capillaries and more mitochondria, HIIT strongly improves how efficiently your existing mitochondria work under high demand.

areas.cardioFitness: HIIT training significantly increases VO2 max, improving cardiovascular capacity, endurance, and overall aerobic fitness.
areas.energy: HIIT improves the working capacity of existing mitochondria and the ability to generate energy rapidly at high intensity, increasing metabolic efficiency when demand is high.
areas.longevity: Higher VO2 max is one of the strongest predictors of long-term health and survival, making HIIT a valuable longevity stimulus when recovery is managed well.

running_volume_aerobic.title: Running volume for aerobic capacity
running_volume_aerobic.description: Running volume is about the total amount of running you accumulate over a week. In practice, a large share of that volume should still be done in Zone 2, otherwise the total stress can become too high for recovery, joints, and the nervous system. Unlike Zone 2, which mainly describes the intensity of an individual session, running volume is more about building durability, tissue tolerance, and aerobic capacity through consistent total workload over time. When increased gradually, it can also strengthen tendons, ligaments, and tissue tolerance around the joints.

areas.cardioFitness: Regular running volume strengthens the heart, increases stroke volume, and improves overall cardiovascular endurance and aerobic capacity.
areas.energy: Aerobic running improves fat oxidation, enhances mitochondrial function, and increases sustained energy levels for daily activities.

zone2_slow_running.title: Zone 2 / slow running
zone2_slow_running.description: Easy Zone 2 running is one of the most useful health habits because it gives you a large cardio-metabolic return without excessive stress. The goal is not speed or mileage, but a relaxed pace where you can still speak in full sentences. Zone 2 increases the number of capillaries feeding the muscles and stimulates the creation of more mitochondria, making muscles better at receiving oxygen and producing aerobic energy. This is different from running volume: Zone 2 is primarily about keeping effort easy enough, while running volume is about how much total running you accumulate over time.

areas.cardioFitness: Slow Zone 2 running strengthens the heart and increases capillary density in working muscles, improving oxygen delivery and aerobic endurance.
areas.energy: Easy aerobic movement stimulates the creation of more mitochondria and improves day-to-day energy with relatively low strain.

magnesium.title: Magnesium
magnesium.description: Magnesium is an essential mineral that plays a vital role in muscle relaxation, nervous system function, and sleep quality. It helps the body regulate stress hormones and promotes deeper, more restorative sleep.

areas.sleepQuality: Magnesium improves sleep quality by regulating melatonin and promoting muscle relaxation.
areas.nervousSystem: Magnesium supports the nervous system by regulating neurotransmitters and reducing stress.
areas.energy: Magnesium is necessary for energy production and reduces fatigue by supporting ATP synthesis.

pumpkinSeeds.details: 30 g roasted pumpkin seeds give around 150 mg magnesium.

almonds.details: 30 g almonds contribute roughly 80 mg magnesium.

darkChocolate.details: 30 g 70-85% cacao dark chocolate supplies about 65 mg magnesium.

blackBeans.details: 1 cup cooked black beans (~170 g) yields about 120 mg magnesium.

avocado.details: One medium avocado offers roughly 60 mg magnesium.

spinach.details: 1 cup cooked spinach (~180 g) provides about 150 mg magnesium.

zinc_comprehensive_support.title: Zinc for immune resilience
zinc_comprehensive_support.description: Zinc is a trace mineral critical for immune defense, tissue repair, hormone balance, and normal hair growth. Highly absorbable forms can help maintain resilience during stress and intense training, and low zinc status can contribute to hair shedding and poorer hair quality.

areas.immuneSupport: Zinc supports innate and adaptive immunity by regulating cytokine signaling and white blood cell activity.
areas.nervousSystem: Adequate zinc helps maintain neurotransmitter balance, supporting mood and stress tolerance.
areas.energy: Zinc is required for hundreds of enzymatic reactions linked to energy metabolism and recovery.
areas.womenHealth: Zinc is needed for normal reproductive function, cell division and immune function. Zinc is also important for hair growth and skin health.
areas.menHealth: Zinc is needed for normal reproductive function. Zinc deficiency can affect hormone function, but extra zinc is not an established treatment for testosterone deficiency when intake is already adequate.

oysters.details: Three medium oysters deliver about 30 mg zinc.

beef.details: A 120 g portion of beef provides roughly 5 mg zinc.

pumpkinSeeds.details: 30 g pumpkin seeds add about 2-3 mg zinc.

chickpeas.details: 1 cup cooked chickpeas (~170 g) gives around 2.5 mg zinc.

cashews.details: 30 g cashews supply roughly 1.6 mg zinc.

selenium_thyroid_antioxidant.title: Selenium for thyroid and antioxidant defense
selenium_thyroid_antioxidant.description: Selenium powers glutathione-based antioxidant enzymes and supports the conversion of thyroid hormones, helping maintain immunity, energy, stress tolerance, and normal hair growth. Low selenium status or impaired thyroid function can negatively affect hair quality.

areas.immuneSupport: Selenium supports antibody production and regulates inflammation, bolstering immune resilience.
areas.energy: Selenium-dependent enzymes activate thyroid hormones that drive metabolic energy and mitochondrial efficiency.
areas.nervousSystem: Selenium protects neurons from oxidative stress and supports balanced mood and stress responses.

brazilNuts.details: One Brazil nut delivers 60-90 μg selenium; limit to 1-2 per day.

sardines.details: 100 g sardines provide about 45 μg selenium.

eggs.details: Two eggs supply roughly 28 μg selenium.

shiitakeMushrooms.details: 100 g cooked shiitake mushrooms give around 20 μg selenium.

sunflowerSeeds.details: 30 g sunflower seeds add about 18 μg selenium.

iodine_thyroid_balance.title: Iodine for thyroid balance
iodine_thyroid_balance.description: Iodine supplies the raw material for thyroid hormones, helping maintain metabolic drive, immune resilience, clear thinking, and normal hair growth. When thyroid function is suboptimal, hair density and hair quality often suffer.

areas.energy: Adequate iodine keeps T3 and T4 production robust, sustaining metabolic energy throughout the day.
areas.immuneSupport: Balanced thyroid hormones modulate immune signaling and help the body respond appropriately to stressors.
areas.nervousSystem: Iodine supports nervous system stability by maintaining hormone balance that affects mood, focus, and thermoregulation.

iodizedSeaSalt.details: Half a teaspoon of iodized sea salt provides close to 150 μg iodine.

fortifiedDairy.details: A 250 ml glass of fortified milk or fortified plant milk can deliver around 40-60 μg iodine.

eggs.details: Two eggs provide roughly 50 μg iodine.

cod.details: A 120 g cod fillet offers about 110 μg iodine.

betaine_cardiovascular.title: Betaine
betaine_cardiovascular.description: Betaine supports cardiovascular function and physical performance.

rhodiola_adaptogen.title: Rhodiola
rhodiola_adaptogen.description:
Origin: Rhodiola rosea, also called rose root or arctic root, grows in cold regions and at high altitudes. Its root and rhizome are used in extracts that may contain rosavins and salidroside. Species, extraction method, and standardization affect composition, so products are not necessarily comparable.

Research: Rhodiola has been studied for stress-related fatigue and mental performance. A small placebo-controlled trial of a standardized extract reported improvements in some fatigue and attention measures after four weeks. Many studies are small, short, or methodologically weak. EMA’s assessment for temporary relief of stress symptoms such as fatigue rests on traditional use rather than sufficiently strong clinical evidence.

Stress and nervous-system hypotheses: The term adaptogen describes substances proposed to influence adaptation to stress. Rhodiola research examines stress signaling and neurotransmitters, among other mechanisms. This does not establish that the plant normalizes stress hormones or corrects an imbalance in every user.

Mitochondria and energy: In cell and mouse models of oxygen and energy deprivation, salidroside affected mitochondrial quality control, including through the energy sensor AMPK. This generates hypotheses about cellular responses to metabolic stress. Experiments with an isolated compound in injured cells do not establish that rhodiola supplements increase ATP production, everyday energy, or endurance in humans.

User reports: On forums such as Reddit, some people describe more energy, motivation, better focus, and less perceived stress. Others notice no difference or feel that an initial effect fades. There are also accounts of feeling overstimulated, more anxious or irritable, and having trouble sleeping, sometimes after an initially positive experience.

These are personal experiences, not controlled studies. They do not establish how common the effects are or whether rhodiola caused them. Extract differences, other supplements or medication, sleep, and expectations may influence the experience. A fading perceived effect also does not prove tolerance or a need to increase the dose.

Uncertainties: Findings for one extract cannot be directly generalized to other products. Lasting improvements in memory, focus, or physical performance have not been established. Persistent or new fatigue warrants assessment of possible causes rather than relying solely on supplements.

Safety: Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding because safety data are lacking. Headache, dizziness, dry mouth, and insomnia may occur; long-term safety is insufficiently characterized. Use in bipolar disorder or a history of mania should be assessed by a clinician, as isolated cases of mania have been reported. Do not combine with antidepressants on your own initiative; a possible interaction with paroxetine has been reported. Chronic illness or regular medication, including blood thinners or anti-seizure drugs, requires individualized assessment. Before surgery, inform the surgical or anesthesia team and follow their instructions about stopping supplements.

areas.nervousSystem:
Rhodiola is being investigated for stress-related fatigue. Small studies of particular standardized extracts suggest possible benefits, but general regulation of the stress system or increased nervous-system resilience has not been established.

Effects on stress signaling and neurotransmitters are possible mechanisms. Perceived stimulation may also involve insomnia or restlessness. Particular caution is needed with bipolar disorder or concurrent antidepressant treatment.
areas.energy:
Rhodiola has mainly been studied for perceived fatigue under stress. Some short trials report improvement, but reduced fatigue is not the same as proven increases in energy production or physical endurance.

In cell and animal models, salidroside affected AMPK and mitochondrial quality control during oxygen and energy deprivation. This is a possible mechanism to investigate, not evidence that ordinary rhodiola supplements increase ATP production in humans.
areas.mind:
Some small trials have examined attention and mental work capacity during stress and fatigue. Certain findings are promising, but short follow-up, small groups, and differences between extracts limit conclusions.

General improvements in memory or concentration in healthy people have not been established. Any benefit may also reflect reduced perceived fatigue rather than a direct enhancement of cognition.

holy_basil_adaptogen.title: Holy Basil (Tulsi)
holy_basil_adaptogen.description: Holy Basil, also known as Tulsi, is an adaptogenic herb revered in traditional medicine for its stress-reducing and immune-supporting properties.

areas.nervousSystem: Holy Basil helps calm the nervous system and reduce stress through its adaptogenic effects.
areas.immuneSupport: Holy Basil supports immune function with its antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties.

reishi_mushroom.title: Reishi
reishi_mushroom.description:
Origin: Reishi, also called lingzhi, is a name used for several closely related Ganoderma mushrooms, including Ganoderma lingzhi and Ganoderma lucidum. They have a long history in East Asian traditions. Extracts may contain beta-glucans and triterpenes; composition varies between fruiting bodies, mycelium, spores, and extraction methods.

Research: Human studies are limited and findings apply to specific preparations. An eight-week placebo-controlled trial in people diagnosed with neurasthenia reported reduced fatigue with a polysaccharide extract. This does not establish that all reishi products increase energy or treat stress and sleep problems. Changes in immune markers have also been investigated, but these alone do not demonstrate fewer infections or better health.

Hypotheses: Beta-glucans and other constituents may influence immune-cell signaling. Cell and animal studies also examine inflammatory pathways and oxidative stress. Immune modulation means influencing immune responses; it does not automatically mean that a stronger response is desirable or that immunity is balanced in humans.

Animal studies and autoimmunity: In a mouse model of an MS-like disease (EAE), Ganoderma lucidum powder reduced some disease signs and affected nervous-system inflammation. This generates hypotheses involving microglia, the immune cells of the nervous system, but does not demonstrate safe or effective treatment of MS or other autoimmune diseases in humans.

Safety: Safety data during pregnancy and breastfeeding are insufficient; avoid supplements without a healthcare assessment. Use should be assessed by the treating clinician in autoimmune disease, organ transplantation, or liver or kidney disease, particularly with immunosuppressive treatment. Reishi may increase bleeding risk with blood-thinning medication. Before surgery, inform the surgical or anesthesia team and follow their instructions about stopping supplements. Nausea and insomnia may occur. Isolated cases of liver injury have been reported, although causality is often uncertain.

areas.immuneSupport:
Reishi beta-glucans and triterpenes are being studied for effects on immune-cell signaling and inflammation. Some human studies have measured changes in immune markers, but prevention of infections or a general improvement in immune function has not been established.

Findings from animal models of autoimmunity generate hypotheses. Autoimmune disease or immunosuppressive treatment requires clinician assessment; immune effects are not automatically beneficial.
areas.nervousSystem:
Reishi is traditionally used for calm and sleep. Research examines inflammatory signaling and immune cells in the nervous system, but much of the mechanistic evidence comes from cell and animal studies.

A short human trial of a particular polysaccharide extract reported reduced fatigue in neurasthenia. This cannot be generalized to all products or considered an established treatment for stress, anxiety, or sleep problems. Insomnia has also been reported as an adverse effect.

lions_mane_mushroom.title: Lion's Mane
lions_mane_mushroom.description:
Origin: Lion’s Mane (Hericium erinaceus) is an edible mushroom with long white spines. Supplements may contain fruiting bodies, mycelium, or different extracts. Hericenones and erinacines are compound groups under investigation; composition varies with cultivation, mushroom part, and manufacturing. Products are therefore not necessarily comparable.

Research: A small placebo-controlled trial in 30 people with mild cognitive impairment reported better cognitive test scores during 16 weeks of use; scores declined after discontinuation. This does not establish dementia prevention. Small trials in younger adults have produced mixed findings, with possible improvements in individual tasks but no reliable general evidence for better memory or focus. Larger, independent studies are needed.

Nervous-system hypotheses: Laboratory studies have found that some extracts and isolated compounds affect nerve growth factor (NGF) and nerve-cell projections. NGF contributes to the survival and function of certain neurons. These findings have prompted interest in neural plasticity but do not establish that supplements repair nerves or create new neurons in the human brain. Effects may differ across extracts and experimental models.

User reports: On forums such as Reddit, some people describe better focus, less brain fog, and improved mood, while others notice no effect. There are also accounts of anxiety, sleep problems, brain fog, reduced libido, emotional blunting, or a reduced ability to experience pleasure (anhedonia). Some describe symptoms persisting after discontinuation.

These experiences deserve attention, but forum reports cannot establish causality, frequency, or expected duration. Selection of people posting, product composition, other substances, and concurrent symptoms may influence the picture. No established explanation for the reported persistent symptoms exists; NGF hypotheses should not be presented as proof of a particular injury mechanism.

Safety: Abdominal discomfort, nausea, and skin rash have been reported in clinical studies. Avoid with a known allergy to the mushroom. Safety of concentrated supplements during pregnancy, breastfeeding, and long-term use is insufficiently characterized. Discuss use with healthcare professionals if you have a chronic condition or take regular medication. Before surgery, inform the surgical or anesthesia team and follow their instructions. For new or persistent psychological or neurological symptoms, stop the supplement and contact a healthcare professional.

areas.mind:
Small human trials have examined memory, attention, and perceived stress. A trial in mild cognitive impairment reported improved test scores during use, but this does not establish dementia prevention or general cognitive enhancement in healthy people.

Personal reports describe less brain fog and better focus as well as opposite experiences. They can generate research questions but cannot establish how common an effect is or who will benefit from supplementation.
areas.nervousSystem:
Some Lion’s Mane extracts and compounds such as erinacines are being investigated for effects on NGF and nerve-cell projections. NGF is a signaling molecule contributing to the survival and function of certain neurons. Evidence mainly comes from cell and animal studies; repair of nerve injuries in humans has not been established.

Online forums include reports of anxiety, sleep problems, emotional blunting, and sometimes persistent symptoms after discontinuation. Causality and mechanisms are uncertain, and these reports should not be equated with clinically demonstrated nerve injury.

chaga_mushroom.title: Chaga
chaga_mushroom.description:
Origin: Chaga (Inonotus obliquus) forms dark, hard growths, mainly on birch trees. The material is used for tea, powders, and extracts. Polysaccharide, polyphenol, and triterpene content varies with growing conditions, raw material, and extraction. Tea, powder, and concentrated extracts are therefore not equivalent products.

Research: Evidence of benefits in humans is very limited. Most research comes from cell and animal experiments. Clinical evidence is insufficient to establish improved immunity, increased energy, or disease prevention. Effects on cancer cells in the laboratory do not demonstrate cancer prevention or treatment in humans.

Cell-protection and immunity hypotheses: Extracts and isolated constituents have shown antioxidant activity and effects on immune cells and inflammatory pathways experimentally. Antioxidant activity in a test tube does not establish that compounds reach relevant tissues or provide a health benefit. Immune modulation should not be equated with stronger or better balanced immunity.

Energy and animal studies: Mouse experiments with Chaga polysaccharides have found longer swimming times and changes in liver and muscle glycogen stores. These generate hypotheses about fuel metabolism and physical fatigue but do not establish increased ATP production, everyday energy, or endurance in humans.

User reports: On forums such as Reddit, some people describe reduced fatigue or perceived improvements in skin or digestion. Others notice no clear effect. There are also accounts of diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and anxiety. These reports can generate research questions but cannot establish causality, frequency, or benefit from a particular product. Product composition, other supplements, and concurrent symptoms make experiences difficult to compare.

Oxalates and kidneys: Chaga can contain high levels of oxalate. Published case reports describe oxalate crystals and severe kidney injury following high or prolonged intake of Chaga powder; some patients required dialysis. These are medical case reports, not merely forum accounts. They do not establish the magnitude of risk with other products or lower intake, nor can a generally safe supplement dose be inferred from them. People with kidney disease or previous oxalate stones should avoid Chaga without assessment by a kidney specialist.

Safety: Safety data during pregnancy, breastfeeding, and long-term use are insufficient. Possible additive effects with blood-thinning and glucose-lowering medication warrant caution; clinical significance is not fully characterized. Autoimmune disease, transplantation, or immunosuppressive treatment requires clinician assessment. Before surgery, inform the surgical or anesthesia team and follow their instructions about stopping supplements.

areas.immuneSupport:
Chaga extracts and polysaccharides have affected immune cells and inflammatory pathways in cell and animal experiments. This generates hypotheses rather than demonstrating fewer infections or improved immune health in humans.

Influencing an immune response is not automatically beneficial. Use in autoimmune disease or during immunosuppressive treatment should be assessed by the treating clinician.
areas.energy:
Mouse studies of particular Chaga polysaccharides have found longer swimming times and increased liver and muscle glycogen stores. Glycogen is a carbohydrate reserve that can be used as fuel. These findings generate hypotheses about energy metabolism but do not establish improved ATP production or reduced fatigue in humans.

Some users report more energy, while others notice no effect or experience digestive discomfort. Clinical evidence is insufficient to recommend Chaga as a fatigue treatment, and kidney risks need to be considered.

cordyceps_adaptogen.title: Cordyceps
cordyceps_adaptogen.description:
Origin: Cordyceps is a name used for different fungi and cultivated products. Ophiocordyceps sinensis is the traditional caterpillar fungus from Asian highlands, whereas Cordyceps militaris is a different species often cultivated for supplements. Fermented mycelium products such as Cs-4 are also used. Species, mushroom part, and extraction method affect composition; products are not interchangeable in research.

Research: Small human trials have investigated physical performance with mixed findings. A trial in older adults found improvements in some threshold measures but no increase in VO₂max. A trial in endurance-trained cyclists found no improvement in aerobic capacity or performance after five weeks of Cs-4. Other small trials suggest possible benefits, but evidence does not establish that all products improve energy or fitness.

Energy hypotheses: Cordycepin, a compound particularly studied from C. militaris, resembles the nucleoside adenosine. In cell experiments its metabolites can influence AMPK, part of cellular energy signaling. This is not equivalent to supplying ATP or demonstrating increased energy production. Findings with isolated cordycepin cannot be directly generalized to mushroom extracts or everyday energy in humans.

Immune function: Cell and animal research shows effects on immune cells and inflammatory signaling. Immune modulation does not automatically mean stronger or better balanced immunity. Ordinary supplements have not been established to prevent infections or treat autoimmune disease.

User reports: On forums such as Reddit, some people describe more energy, better exercise endurance, or improved mood. Others notice little effect or feel it fades. There are also accounts of anxiety, restlessness, and sleep difficulties. Some people also take caffeine or other products, making experiences harder to interpret.

Personal reports can generate research questions but cannot establish causality, frequency, or duration. Feeling more energetic does not necessarily mean better recovery or an ability to tolerate greater exertion.

Safety: Safety data during pregnancy, breastfeeding, and long-term use are limited. Chronic illness, autoimmune disease, transplantation, or regular medication warrants healthcare assessment. Particular caution is needed with glucose-lowering and blood-thinning drugs because additive effects are possible; clinical risk is not fully characterized. Before surgery, inform the surgical or anesthesia team and follow their instructions about stopping supplements. For new or persistent symptoms, stop the supplement and contact a healthcare professional.

areas.energy:
Cordyceps is being studied for fatigue and physical work capacity, but a general energy-enhancing effect has not been established. In cell experiments, cordycepin can affect AMPK and the metabolism of compounds resembling cellular energy nucleotides. This does not demonstrate that supplements replenish ATP or improve mitochondrial energy production in humans.

User reports describe increased energy, no effect, or overactivation with anxiety and sleep problems. Product differences, caffeine, other substances, and sleep may influence the experience.
areas.cardioFitness:
Small trials have examined oxygen uptake, ventilatory thresholds, and endurance with mixed findings. Some report improvements in individual measures, while a trial in trained cyclists found no improvement in aerobic capacity or performance. Results for one species or mycelium product do not automatically apply to other Cordyceps supplements.

The connection mainly concerns possible physical work capacity, not proven protection against heart attacks or other cardiovascular disease.
areas.immuneSupport:
Cordyceps extracts and their constituents affect immune cells in cell and animal experiments. Such changes are of research interest but do not establish fewer infections or better immune health in humans.

Immune effects should not automatically be considered beneficial in autoimmune disease or during immunosuppressive treatment. Use should be assessed by the treating clinician.

zone2_mitochondrial_base.title: Zone 2 for a mitochondrial base
zone2_mitochondrial_base.description: Zone 2 training builds your aerobic foundation by increasing mitochondrial density, capillarization, and fat oxidation. In practice, that means more capillaries feeding the muscles and more mitochondria inside the muscle cells. The goal is a steady, conversational pace where you can speak in full sentences and keep intensity stable over time.

areas.cardioFitness: Zone 2 improves aerobic capacity through increased stroke volume, higher capillary density, and more efficient oxygen delivery to working muscles.
areas.energy: Consistent Zone 2 supports mitochondrial biogenesis, meaning the creation of more mitochondria, and improves energy metabolism for more sustainable energy during training and daily life.
areas.longevity: Maintaining aerobic base and mitochondrial function is strongly linked to healthier aging, higher resilience, and better long-term physical capacity.

zone2_mitochondrial_base.analyzePrompt: Analyze the user's training pattern and determine whether they have enough low-intensity aerobic volume (Zone 2) to support mitochondrial development.

fascia_strength_whole_body_variation.title: 4-5 training modalities for whole-body fascia strength
fascia_strength_whole_body_variation.description: For long-term resilience, avoid repeating only one training pattern. Aim for at least 4-5 different activity types each week, for example: strength, Zone 2 cardio, impact/plyometric loading, rotational or unilateral work, and mobility/balance. This creates varied mechanical signals that support fascia quality, tendon and ligament tolerance, bone remodeling, and whole-body muscle function.

areas.longevity: Training variety across the week helps preserve movement capacity, connective tissue quality, and functional independence as you age.
areas.strength: Different loading patterns improve force transfer through fascia and build stronger, more resilient muscles, tendons, ligaments, and bones.
areas.nervousSystem: Changing training stimulus improves coordination and motor adaptability while reducing repetitive stress on the nervous system.

fasted_aerobic_training.title: Fasted aerobic training
fasted_aerobic_training.description: Low-intensity training with low glycogen availability (e.g., before breakfast) can stimulate fat metabolism and mitochondrial adaptations. Use selectively and primarily in Zone 2 — not for hard intervals.

areas.energy: Training with low glycogen availability may improve fat oxidation and stimulate mitochondrial signaling pathways linked to endurance adaptation.
areas.cardioFitness: When kept low intensity, this can improve aerobic robustness without compromising quality in high-intensity sessions when periodized correctly.

vigorous_exercise_lactate.title: Vigorous exercise and lactate
vigorous_exercise_lactate.description: Brief periods of vigorous exercise can rapidly increase lactate production. Lactate is not simply a waste product – it can be used as fuel and also acts as a signaling molecule throughout the body. Short bouts of higher-intensity activity can therefore be a valuable complement to moderate aerobic exercise for cardiovascular, metabolic and brain health.

areas.cardioFitness: Vigorous activity provides a strong stimulus to the heart and circulatory system in a short amount of time and can help maintain or improve cardiorespiratory fitness and cardiovascular health.
areas.energy: As exercise intensity increases, lactate production rises. Lactate can be transported between tissues and used as fuel, making it an important part of energy metabolism during physical activity.
areas.mind: Exercise-generated lactate can be used as fuel by the brain and also acts as a signaling molecule. Lactate signaling has been linked to BDNF and processes involved in neuroplasticity, which may be one mechanism through which exercise supports brain health.

vigorous_exercise_lactate.analyzePrompt: Analyze the user's current activity level and fitness and suggest a safe way to incorporate brief periods of vigorous activity that can increase lactate production. Focus on cardiovascular, metabolic and brain health rather than athletic performance.

coffee_polyphenols_longevity.title: Coffee and polyphenols for long-term health
coffee_polyphenols_longevity.description: Coffee is a significant source of polyphenols, particularly chlorogenic acids. Regular coffee consumption has been associated with lower risk of several chronic diseases and reduced mortality in large observational studies. The benefits do not appear to be solely due to caffeine, as decaffeinated coffee has also been linked to health benefits.

areas.cardioFitness: Moderate coffee consumption has been associated with lower risk of cardiovascular disease in observational studies. Coffee polyphenols may affect vascular function, inflammation, and oxidative stress, although caffeine can temporarily raise blood pressure in some individuals.
areas.energy: Coffee contains bioactive compounds such as chlorogenic acids that can influence glucose and energy metabolism. Regular coffee consumption has also been linked to lower risk of type 2 diabetes in observational studies.
areas.mind: Regular coffee consumption has been associated with lower risk of certain neurodegenerative diseases in observational studies. Coffee contains several bioactive compounds beyond caffeine, and both caffeine and polyphenols may contribute to the effects.

nitrate_no_efficiency.title: Nitrate and nitric oxide for vascular health
nitrate_no_efficiency.description:
Beetroot, rocket and spinach contain nitrate that can contribute to nitric oxide (NO) formation. Beetroot juice has been studied for both blood pressure and exercise performance. Nitrate content is the key quantity when comparing a product with research – a given weight of beetroot powder does not establish its nitrate dose.

From the mouth to blood vessels: Some nitrate is concentrated in saliva. Bacteria on the tongue convert it to nitrite, which can subsequently form NO, including in acidic and low-oxygen conditions. This differs from NO synthesis from arginine. Govoni and colleagues showed in 2008 that antibacterial mouthwash markedly reduced the rise in blood nitrite after nitrate intake (PMID 18793740). Do not change prescribed oral care to enhance a supplement’s effects.

Blood pressure – promising but inconsistent: Kapil and colleagues randomised 68 people with hypertension to 250 ml of beetroot juice daily or nitrate-depleted placebo juice for four weeks. The study reported lower blood pressure with nitrate (Hypertension, 2015; PMID 25421976). In contrast, Bondonno and colleagues found no reduction in home or ambulatory blood pressure after one week of nitrate-rich juice in treated hypertensive participants (2015; PMID 26135348). Responses therefore vary across people and protocols. Lower blood pressure in a short trial does not itself establish fewer heart attacks or strokes over the long term.

Endurance and oxygen cost: Bailey and colleagues showed in 2009 that nitrate-rich beetroot juice could reduce the oxygen cost of a given cycling workload and extend time to exhaustion in a laboratory test (Journal of Applied Physiology; DOI 10.1152/japplphysiol.00722.2009). This does not automatically translate into the same improvement in competition. Later evidence syntheses indicate that effects depend on factors including test type and training status; not everyone performs better, and an acute effect is not the same as greater long-term training adaptation.

Amounts and timing in research: The Australian Institute of Sport describes approximately 6–8 mmol of nitrate, around 350–500 mg, about 2–3 hours before activity as common in sports studies. This describes research protocols, not a daily nutrition target or personal dosing recommendation. Content varies between beetroot, juices and extracts; more is not necessarily better.

Practical use and safety: Beetroot and leafy vegetables can be part of ordinary meals without a concentrated supplement. Juice may cause gastrointestinal discomfort and temporary red discolouration of urine or stools. Discuss concentrated products with a healthcare professional if you have low blood pressure, take blood pressure medicines or have kidney disease. Do not replace prescribed treatment. Do not self-dose nitrite or chemical nitrate products; long-term use of concentrated supplements is less well studied than short trials.

areas.cardioFitness: Nitrate-rich beetroot juice has lowered blood pressure in some randomised trials, but not all. Supplements have not been shown to prevent heart attacks or strokes and do not replace hypertension treatment.
areas.energy: In some experiments, nitrate reduces the muscular oxygen cost of a given workload and improves endurance. It is not a general energy boost, and effects vary with training status and activity.

beets.details: Beetroot provides nitrate and can be part of ordinary meals. Nitrate content varies; a serving does not automatically match the amount in a standardised beetroot shot.

arugula.details: Rocket is a nitrate-rich leafy vegetable suitable for salads and other meals. Content varies with growing and storage conditions, so a given weight does not provide an exact nitrate dose.

spinach.details: Spinach provides nitrate and other nutrients. Include it as part of a varied vegetable intake; nitrate content varies and is not a fixed daily target.

l_carnitine_fat_transport.title: L-carnitine and fat transport
l_carnitine_fat_transport.description: L-carnitine is involved in transporting fatty acids into mitochondria. Effects on endurance vary between individuals and are more likely to appear with longer-term use alongside a well-structured training and nutrition plan.

areas.energy: Supports pathways involved in fat metabolism and may contribute to more efficient energy supply at low-to-moderate intensity.
areas.cardioFitness: In some cases, it may support endurance by improving fat utilization and reducing glycogen stress during longer sessions.

sauna_mitochondrial_adaptation.title: Sauna for recovery and endurance adaptation
sauna_mitochondrial_adaptation.description: Heat exposure (such as sauna) can act as a hormetic stressor and support heat adaptation, circulation, and recovery. Many endurance athletes use sauna as a training adjunct, especially during higher-volume phases.

areas.energy: Heat can stimulate stress-response pathways and cellular adaptation, supporting resilience and recovery when dosed appropriately.
areas.cardioFitness: Heat acclimation can improve plasma volume and circulatory efficiency, potentially supporting endurance and heat tolerance.

cold_exposure_timing.title: Cold exposure: timing for performance
cold_exposure_timing.description: Cold exposure can increase alertness and stress resilience, but doing it immediately after hard training may interfere with adaptation signals in some cases. The strategy is to time cold exposure to support recovery without ‘stealing’ training gains.

areas.strength: Smart timing can let you use cold for perceived recovery without unnecessarily blunting strength and growth signaling.
areas.cardioFitness: Cold can be used for nervous system regulation and resilience, but should be periodized around key workouts to preserve training quality.

co2_tolerance_breathing.title: CO₂ tolerance and breathing for running
co2_tolerance_breathing.description: CO₂ tolerance influences breathing drive and how efficiently you ventilate at higher intensities. Breathing control and gradual CO₂ exposure can reduce perceived breath stress and improve running economy for some people.

areas.cardioFitness: Better breathing control can improve ventilation patterns and reduce ‘panic breathing’ at high intensity, supporting endurance performance.
areas.energy: More efficient breathing work can reduce the energy cost of ventilation and free capacity for working muscles.

astaxanthin_recovery_antioxidant.title: Astaxanthin
astaxanthin_recovery_antioxidant.description:
Astaxanthin is a red-orange, fat-soluble carotenoid produced by organisms including the microalga Haematococcus pluvialis and found in foods such as salmon and shrimp. Supplements are often made from this alga.

Membranes and mitochondria: Cell and mitochondrial membranes consist largely of a double layer of lipids. Oxidation of these lipids (lipid peroxidation) can affect membrane structure and function. Laboratory studies using model membranes have found that astaxanthin reduced this oxidation and helped preserve membrane structure. Experiments in vitamin E-deficient rats have also shown protection against oxidative damage in mitochondria. This provides a possible rationale for interest in astaxanthin for recovery, but does not itself establish that supplements protect human membranes or improve energy production. The molecule’s location within membranes varies between experimental models.

Tocotrienols and vitamin E: Tocotrienols belong to the vitamin E family and have an unsaturated side chain, unlike the saturated side chain of tocopherols. This difference may affect how the molecules move and interact with membrane lipids. Laboratory studies have demonstrated antioxidant effects, making tocotrienols of interest in research on membranes and oxidative stress. A complementary effect alongside astaxanthin is a hypothesis; the combination has not been established to improve membrane protection or recovery in humans. Tocotrienols should also not be equated with alpha-tocopherol, the form established to meet human vitamin E requirements.

Research: Human studies have produced mixed findings for recovery and endurance. Some report lower markers of muscle damage, which does not necessarily mean less soreness or better performance. Evidence is insufficient to recommend a particular combination with vitamin E or timing around exercise.

Hypotheses: Antioxidant effects and changes in inflammatory signaling have been observed in cell and animal studies. Improved mitochondrial function or energy levels in humans have not been established.

Animal studies and autoimmunity: In mouse models of an MS-like disease (EAE) and experimentally induced immune-mediated liver inflammation, astaxanthin reduced some disease signs and inflammatory markers. Effects on cells including T cells suggest hypotheses about immune modulation, but do not establish astaxanthin as a treatment for autoimmune diseases in humans.

Safety: Safety data during pregnancy and breastfeeding are insufficient; avoid supplements without a healthcare assessment. Discuss use with your treating clinician if you have a chronic condition, particularly autoimmune disease, impaired kidney or liver function, or take regular medication. These are precautions reflecting limited knowledge, not evidence that these conditions are generally contraindications. Before surgery, inform the surgical or anesthesia team and follow their instructions about stopping supplements.

areas.strength: Some studies report lower markers of muscle damage, but benefits for soreness, recovery, and strength development remain uncertain.
areas.energy:
Mitochondria convert energy from food into ATP, which powers processes including muscle work and cellular maintenance. In the inner mitochondrial membrane, the electron transport chain builds a proton gradient – a difference in electrical charge and acidity – that ATP synthase uses to produce ATP. Oxidative damage to membrane lipids and proteins can disrupt this process.

Astaxanthin is of interest because cell studies have found that it helped preserve mitochondrial membrane potential and respiration under oxidative stress. The hypothesis is that protecting membranes and enzymes may help sustain energy production under stress. However, supplements have not been established to increase ATP production, reduce fatigue, or improve everyday energy in humans.
areas.cardioFitness:
Astaxanthin is being studied for possible effects on cardiovascular health through oxidative stress, blood lipids, and vascular function. A small randomized trial in people with mildly elevated triglycerides found lower triglycerides and higher HDL in some dose groups. Other trials have not shown the same benefit; a one-year trial in kidney transplant recipients found no improvement in arterial stiffness or vascular function. Blood pressure findings are also mixed.

The hypothesis is that reduced oxidation of blood lipids and effects on the endothelium, the inner lining of blood vessels, may be beneficial. However, supplements have not been established to prevent heart attacks or strokes and do not replace treatment for blood lipids or blood pressure. This connection mainly concerns possible risk markers, not proven improvements in aerobic fitness.

astaxanthin_recovery_antioxidant.analyzePrompt: Describe evidence and uncertainties about astaxanthin in relation to the user’s recovery questions. Distinguish human studies from cell and animal research. Do not present treatment of autoimmune disease, a dose, a particular vitamin E combination, or timing around exercise as scientifically established. Refer disease, medication, pregnancy, breastfeeding, or planned surgery to individualized healthcare assessment.

intermittent_fasting_12h.title: Intermittent fasting 12:12
intermittent_fasting_12h.description: Fasting 12 hours per day (e.g., 19:00–07:00) is a mild form of intermittent fasting that can support digestion, blood sugar balance, and energy levels. It is easy to implement and suitable for most adults.

areas.energy: 12-hour fasting can contribute to more stable energy levels by giving the body time to recover between meals.
areas.digestiveHealth: A longer overnight fast gives the digestive system a break and can improve gut health and metabolism.

intermittent_fasting_16_8.title: Intermittent fasting 16:8
intermittent_fasting_16_8.description: 16:8 means fasting for 16 hours and eating within an 8-hour window (e.g., 12:00–20:00). This method can promote fat burning, insulin sensitivity, and metabolic health. Suitable for those who want to take fasting a step further.

areas.energy: 16:8 fasting can enhance the body's ability to use fat as fuel and provide more consistent energy throughout the day.
areas.digestiveHealth: A longer fasting window can give the gut more time to recover and support a healthy gut microbiome.

habitTargets.description: Practise balance in minimalist shoes on varied terrain for 5 minutes a day.

foot_balance_training.title: How shoes affect balance and foot sensation
foot_balance_training.description: Shoes that squeeze the feet can restrict toe movement and make it harder for the foot to adapt to the ground. Stiff, thick soles can reduce sensory input from the ground and limit natural foot movement. The nervous system then receives less varied information from the feet when coordinating balance and body position. Walking exclusively on flat ground also provides less variety than grass, gravel and woodland trails. Shoe fit, flexibility and ground contact therefore matter for how the feet, muscles and nervous system work together.

areas.strength: Varied terrain challenges the muscles of the feet and lower legs as you stabilize your body and adjust your steps.
areas.nervousSystem: Varied sensory input from the feet challenges the nervous system’s coordination of balance, body position and movement.

near_infrared_red_light.title: Near Infrared / Red Light
near_infrared_red_light.description:
Red light and near infrared (NIR) are used in photobiomodulation (PBM). LEDs or low-power lasers illuminate tissue to influence biological signalling, rather than aiming for substantial heating. Common wavelengths are approximately 630–670 nm for red light and 800–850 nm for NIR, although devices and research protocols vary. NIR is invisible and can generally reach deeper than red light; the amount reaching a particular tissue also depends on skin, fat layers and distance.

Mitochondria and energy: One proposed mechanism involves cytochrome c oxidase, an enzyme in the mitochondrial electron transport chain. Researchers investigate whether light can alter nitric oxide binding, ATP production and signalling through small amounts of reactive oxygen species. These mechanisms are biologically interesting, but cell and animal experiments do not establish that a light panel reliably increases energy production throughout the human body.

Muscles and recovery: Studies have investigated treatment before or after exercise for muscle fatigue, soreness and performance. Some report positive results, but findings are mixed and depend on dose, treatment area and exercise type. An improvement in an endurance test does not automatically mean greater muscle growth or better long-term fitness. PBM does not replace exercise, sleep or adequate nutrition.

Skin: Red light is also studied for skin texture and fine lines, including possible effects on collagen-related processes. Some treatments may produce modest improvements, but home masks, panels and clinical lasers have different properties and cannot be treated as equivalent. Skin results do not establish how effectively a product reaches muscle.

Dose matters: Wavelength, power per unit area, exposure time, distance and treatment area influence results. More light is not always better, and the same number of minutes can deliver very different doses with different devices. There is therefore no universal treatment time for every product or purpose. Follow the specific device instructions rather than transferring a research protocol directly to a different panel.

Safety: Do not look directly into the light source and use the eye protection specified by the manufacturer; invisible NIR is not automatically safe for the eyes. Stop if you experience discomfort, skin irritation or excessive heat. Consult a healthcare professional before use if you have an eye condition, photosensitivity or take medicines that increase sensitivity to light. This tip concerns general PBM, not self-treatment of the eyes.

areas.energy: Researchers investigate effects on mitochondrial signalling and ATP production. Promising mechanisms do not establish a reliable increase in whole-body energy from home treatment.
areas.strength: Some studies report reduced muscle fatigue or improved recovery, but results vary with dose and exercise type. Long-term strength gains are not guaranteed.

far_infrared_light.title: Far Infrared
far_infrared_light.description:
Far infrared (FIR) radiation is used in infrared saunas. It is absorbed mainly by water in superficial skin tissues and converted into heat that can then spread further. An infrared sauna can therefore warm the body at a lower air temperature than a traditional sauna. This differs from red light and near infrared, where researchers also study how light affects cellular signalling.

How the body responds: Heat dilates skin blood vessels, increases skin blood flow and may raise heart rate as the body attempts to lose heat. Sweating helps cool the body. The response depends on temperature, duration and equipment; an increased heart rate does not mean that sauna bathing provides the same training effect as physical activity.

Research: In Japan, FIR has been studied as Waon therapy, typically 15 minutes at 60 °C followed by supervised rest. Studies in patients with heart failure have reported improvements in some symptoms and functional measures, but these findings concern specific clinical protocols and cannot be directly applied to home use. How much is due to heat in general and how much is specific to FIR remains uncertain.

Recovery and energy: Warmth may feel relaxing and temporarily relieve stiffness. Evidence that FIR improves muscle growth or long-term performance is limited. Heat stress can activate heat shock proteins that help cells manage damaged proteins, but this mechanism does not establish that a particular infrared sauna improves mitochondrial energy production or extends lifespan.

Practical use and safety: Start cautiously with short sessions and comfortable heat, drink water and stop if you feel dizzy, nauseated or experience palpitations. Avoid alcohol around sauna use. Discuss use with a healthcare professional first if you have cardiovascular disease, low blood pressure, are pregnant or take medicines that affect blood pressure or fluid balance.

areas.energy: Heat activates temperature regulation and may promote relaxation. Heat shock proteins are a possible mechanism, but improved energy production from FIR has not been established.
areas.strength: May provide temporary relaxation and relief from perceived stiffness. Evidence for improved muscle growth and long-term performance is limited.

habitTargets.description: Practise calm nasal breathing for 5 minutes.

nasal_breathing_nitric_oxide.title: Nasal Breathing and Nitric Oxide
nasal_breathing_nitric_oxide.description:
Nasal breathing warms, humidifies and filters inhaled air. It also mixes the air with nitric oxide (NO) from the nose and sinuses. Read the group information for general NO signalling and its connection to medicines such as Viagra.

The sinuses as an NO source: Lundberg and colleagues showed in 1995 that the sinus lining produces high concentrations of NO (Nature Medicine; PMID 7585069). During nasal breathing, some travels with inhaled air into the lungs. Nasal breathing therefore involves transporting existing NO, not simply “producing more NO”.

Oxygenation and circulation: A 1996 physiological study investigated how nasal NO affects pulmonary function. Findings suggested effects on oxygenation and pulmonary vascular resistance in some experiments (Lundberg and colleagues; PMID 8971255). This is interesting but does not establish that five minutes of nasal breathing improves fitness or treats high blood pressure. A 1997 study by Yasuda and colleagues found more NO during nasal breathing with light exercise without corresponding improvements in the measured cardiorespiratory indices.

Humming: Weitzberg and Lundberg reported approximately 15-fold higher nasal exhaled NO during humming than quiet exhalation in 2002 (PMID 12119224). Vibrations increased gas exchange between the sinuses and nasal cavity. This does not mean 15 times more NO in the blood or a 15-fold health benefit; the study measured a local, temporary change.

Practical use: Practise five minutes of comfortable, gentle nasal breathing. You can try a few softly hummed exhalations without straining. The target is a simple breathing habit, not an established NO dose. During intense exercise, mouth breathing may be necessary for adequate ventilation. Do not force nasal breathing with a blocked nose or breathlessness; recurrent breathing difficulties warrant medical assessment.

areas.energy: The nose adds NO to inhaled air, but this does not guarantee improved oxygen uptake, energy or performance. Breathe comfortably and adapt breathing to the activity.
areas.cardioFitness: NO helps regulate vascular tone through cGMP. Nasal NO has been studied for pulmonary effects, but nasal breathing is not an established treatment for hypertension or cardiovascular disease.

lutein_zeaxanthin_eye_health.title: Lutein and Zeaxanthin for Eye Health
lutein_zeaxanthin_eye_health.description: Lutein and zeaxanthin are antioxidants that protect the eyes from harmful light and may reduce the risk of age-related macular degeneration. Found in kale, spinach, and egg yolk.

areas.energy: Supports eye energy metabolism and protection.

msm_joint_health.title: MSM for Joint Health
msm_joint_health.description: MSM (methylsulfonylmethane) is a sulfur-containing compound that may reduce joint pain and support recovery. Commonly used for joint issues and to reduce inflammation, it may also reduce gut inflammation, support mucosal health, and contribute to better digestion. MSM may also provide sulfur for keratin formation, making it relevant for stronger hair and improved hair growth.

areas.strength: Supports joint strength and function.
areas.recovery: May help speed up recovery from joint issues.
areas.immuneSupport: Has anti-inflammatory properties that support immune health.

lighting_hygiene.title: Lighting hygiene
lighting_hygiene.description:
Lighting hygiene means adapting light intensity, colour and timing to the day: brighter days, dim evenings and dark nights.

Morning and daytime: Seek daylight after waking and during the day. Supplement it with adequate indoor task lighting. Blue-enriched white light can support daytime alertness and does not need to be avoided around the clock.

Evening and night: Dim lighting during the last hours before bed. Choose low-intensity warm light and lower screen brightness. Night mode does not eliminate all light effects. Dim amber or red light generally affects circadian timing less, but warm light can still be too bright. Keep the bedroom dark and use dim lighting for safe movement if needed.

LEDs and flicker: LED output can fluctuate rapidly because of drivers and dimming, sometimes through rapid on–off cycles (PWM). Modulation may occur even when light appears steady. Choose stable lighting and compatible dimmers; check dimmed settings too. A warm colour or a “flicker-free” label does not guarantee low modulation. Read more about its effects under Nervous system.

Simple phone check: Record an evenly lit surface in slow motion, ideally at both full and dimmed brightness. Moving dark bands or pulsing may indicate light modulation. Camera settings affect the result: this does not measure modulation levels or health risk, and a recording without bands does not guarantee flicker-free light.

A lamp’s kelvin rating is not the whole picture: intensity at the eyes, spectrum and duration matter too. These suggestions assume a typical daytime schedule; night work may require different timing.

areas.sleepQuality: A clear contrast between daylight and dim evening light supports circadian timing. LED intensity, spectrum and timing matter for melatonin and sleep.
areas.nervousSystem: Light reaching the eyes influences nervous system regulation of alertness and circadian timing. Flicker can place demands on the visual system and cause eyestrain, headaches or migraine symptoms in susceptible people. Certain flashing patterns can trigger seizures in photosensitive epilepsy. Effects depend partly on frequency and modulation depth; not all LED modulation has been shown to produce a general nervous system stress response.

urolithin_a.title: Urolithin A for mitochondrial health
urolithin_a.description: Urolithin A is a metabolite produced by gut bacteria from ellagitannins found in foods like pomegranate. It has been shown to support mitochondrial function, increase energy levels, and promote muscle health by stimulating mitophagy—the process by which cells clear out old mitochondria. Note: Around 60% of the population lack the right gut bacteria to produce urolithin A, so supplementation may be necessary for effect.

areas.energy: Urolithin A may improve cellular energy production by optimizing mitochondrial function.Supports mitophagy and helps maintain healthy, efficient mitochondria in cells.

nutritionFoods.title: Foods that may increase urolithin A

pomegranate.details: Rich in ellagitannins, which are converted to urolithin A by gut bacteria.

walnuts.details: Contain ellagitannins that may contribute to urolithin A formation.

strawberries.details: Provide ellagitannins and other polyphenols that support gut health and urolithin A production.

raspberries.details: A source of ellagitannins and may help with urolithin A formation.

protein_rotation.title: Rotate your protein sources

veganInfo.title: Especially relevant for vegans
veganInfo.description: Plant proteins have varying amino acid profiles. Eating a varied diet and enough protein throughout the day makes it easier to meet your essential amino acid needs.

targets.description: Amino acid targets follow WHO/FAO/UNU mean adult requirements. Methionine + cysteine and phenylalanine + tyrosine are assessed together. Total protein follows your personal protein goal. Presets use 15% of energy and at least 0.83 g/kg per day below age 65. From age 65, the app uses 18% and at least 1.5 g/kg per day. NNR gives a range of 1.2–1.5 g/kg for older adults; the app uses the upper end as its minimum. The weight-based minimum may result in a higher protein share.

protein_rotation.description:
Vary your protein sources throughout the day: pulses, tofu, grains, nuts and seeds, and if you eat them, eggs, dairy or fish. Different sources complement each other’s amino acid profiles. Eat enough energy and protein across the day.

Daily targets use the weight in your profile and WHO/FAO/UNU mean adult amino acid requirements. Methionine is counted together with cysteine, and phenylalanine with tyrosine. These reference values are not individual recommendations or training targets, and do not alone establish whether your total protein intake or absorption is adequate.

The total protein target follows your protein goal in nutrition settings.

areas.strength: Varied protein sources provide essential amino acids for muscle and recovery. WHO targets reflect mean baseline needs, not optimal intake for strength training.
areas.womenHealth: Rotating protein sources helps supply different essential amino acids. Targets reflect adult baseline needs and are not specifically adjusted for pregnancy or breastfeeding.
areas.menHealth: Essential amino acids are needed for protein synthesis. Rotating protein sources is dietary guidance, not treatment for testosterone deficiency.
areas.longevity: A varied diet with enough protein helps meet essential amino acid needs. Individual assessment may be needed, for example in older age or illness.

chickpeas.details: Beans, lentils and peas provide protein and lysine. Include grains throughout the day for variety.

soybeans.details: Soybeans, tofu and tempeh are plant protein sources that provide all nine essential amino acids.

oats.details: Oats and other grains can complement pulses in a varied diet.

eggs.details: Eggs provide all nine essential amino acids if you eat animal foods.
